docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Start minimal, then expand. Your first version should take 20 minutes. Add detail as you discover what's useful.

Be specific about file locations. "I use Dropbox" is less useful than "~/Dropbox/Research/ with subfolders per project containing /code/, /data/, and /docs/."

Include your skill level. A beginner needs explanations; an expert wants efficiency. Don't oversell your skills — Claude will calibrate its responses wrong.

Update when things change. New project? New tool? Update your CLAUDE.md. A stale document is worse than a minimal one.

docs.title: Test It
docs.text:
After creating your CLAUDE.md, start Claude Code and ask:

"What do you know about me and my work?"

Claude should reference information from your file. If it doesn't, check:

  1. File location: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
  2. File name: Must be exactly CLAUDE.md
  3. File contents: Open it and verify it's not empty

docs.title: Model Choice
docs.text:
Claude Code defaults to the Sonnet 4.6 model, which is fast and capable for most tasks. For complex work — long-form writing, nuanced analysis, multi-step reasoning — consider switching to Opus 4.6:

/model opus

Opus 4.6 is more capable but uses more tokens per response (higher cost, faster usage against plan limits). This setting applies to the current session only. Switch back with /model sonnet.

docs.title: Advanced: Project-Specific CLAUDE.md
docs.text:
In addition to your global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, you can create a CLAUDE.md in any project folder. Claude reads both when you start a session in that directory.

How they work together:

File Location Purpose Global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md Who you are — role, preferences, contact info, working style Project my-project/.claude/CLAUDE.md This specific project — team, tools, conventions, file paths

Claude loads the global file first, then the project file. Project instructions can override or extend global ones.

my-project/
├── .claude/
│   └── CLAUDE.md    ← project-specific instructions
├── data/
├── code/
└── docs/

This is useful when you work on multiple projects with different conventions, team members, or tools.

What goes in your CLAUDE.md is sent to the API

Everything in your CLAUDE.md files is included in every conversation with Claude Code. This is how Claude knows about you and your projects. The data is covered by Anthropic's API data policy. Avoid including passwords, API keys, or information you wouldn't want transmitted to a cloud service.

docs.title: Voice & Writing Style
docs.text:
If AI output never quite sounds like your writing — too formal, too hedgy, full of words you'd never use — a voice file fixes that. It's a document that captures your actual writing patterns: sentence structure, vocabulary preferences, a ban list of AI-isms, and annotated examples.

The simplest implementation: save your core voice file to ~/.claude/rules/ and it auto-loads every session, just like other rule files. No @import needed for the fundamentals.

~/.claude/rules/core-voice.md    ← auto-loads every session

For context-specific registers (proposal voice vs. email voice), load those on demand through skills or @voice/ imports in project-level CLAUDE.md files.

Teaching AI your voice — build the voice file step by step, with a fill-in template

docs.title: If you use Codex too: AGENTS.md
docs.text:
Claude reads CLAUDE.md. Codex reads AGENTS.md. The contents are interchangeable — the only difference is the filename each app looks for.

Two copies is the obvious approach and the wrong one: they drift, and the day they disagree you won't know which app read which. Make one file the real one and the other a pointer to it.

Ask your agent to do it, in the folder where the file lives:

Make AGENTS.md a symlink to CLAUDE.md in this folder, so both apps read the same file.

A symlink is a stand-in that points at the real file — open either name and you get the same content. Edit CLAUDE.md and Codex sees the change immediately, because there is only one file.

Which one should be the real file?

Whichever app you use more. If you mostly work in Claude, keep CLAUDE.md real and point AGENTS.md at it, as above. The arrangement is symmetrical; what matters is that exactly one of them holds the text.

The same pattern works for the global file — Claude's at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, Codex's at ~/.codex/AGENTS.md.

docs.title: Downloadable Template & Real Example
docs.text:
• CLAUDE.md Template — The starter file. Fill in the blanks.
  • A Real CLAUDE.md — Annotated — My actual production CLAUDE.md (sanitized), showing what a mature configuration looks like after months of iteration. Study this when you're ready to level up.

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text:
With your CLAUDE.md in place:

  1. Connect external services — Give Claude access to email, docs, and calendar
  2. Explore skills — Download tools that automate common workflows

Yay, my agent knows who I am!

docs.title: AI Integration: Cross-Vendor Critics and Peer Tools
docs.text:
Looking for the revised workflow? Start with the new council guide. This reference describes the existing setup; the preview workflow and file contract are being redesigned before the skills are updated.

A council of four Claudes still shares one model's blind spots. The fix is to swap one seat for Codex or Gemini — same prompt, different vendor, dispatched in the same parallel call. I have caught failures this way that no all-Claude panel surfaced, mostly around empirical claims Claude wanted to believe.

This page covers the integration: which CLIs to install, how /council --peer swaps a Claude critic for a peer-vendor critic, what to do for tools without a CLI (Grok, ChatGPT Deep Research, Perplexity), and the failure modes I've actually hit.

docs.title: Why mix vendors
docs.text:
One model has consistent biases. Four instances of the same model share those biases. The council pattern protects against single-critic blind spots within Claude's distribution — not against the distribution itself.

Mixing vendors is cheap insurance. The peer doesn't need to be smarter; it needs to be different. Codex tends to be sharper on empirical and engineering claims that a confident-sounding Claude may wave through. Gemini's long-context window and search-grounding catch coverage gaps in literature reviews. Neither replaces Claude on this stack — both add a lens Claude alone doesn't bring.

docs.title: A worked example — deep research synthesis
docs.text:
The use I reach for most is multi-source research synthesis, and it's the loop /dr-synthesize runs councils on. Say I'm pulling together evidence on what works to reduce homicide in low-trust urban settings — two reviews, eight RCTs, six quasi-experimental papers, a few policy briefs. Thirty sources. /deep-research produced the raw reports (Claude WebSearch + Codex + Gemini CLI in parallel); /dr-synthesize combined them into one draft. Before I trust the draft enough to send to a co-author or use in a grant, I run a council on it.

Panel: harsh-referee, methodologist, academic-editor — three Claude critics on a four-seat council, with the fourth seat swapped for Gemini (long-context, reads the whole source bundle in one pass).

The three Claude critics give me what they always give me on a literature review: tighter argument structure, sharper claim language, a couple of methodology weaknesses they all converge on. Useful, but not surprising.

The Gemini seat, reading the entire bundle as one corpus, surfaces three things the Claude critics didn't:

  1. Three of the cited hot-spots papers turn out to be follow-ups on a single Bogotá experiment — the "consistent evidence" is less independent than my synthesis implied.
  2. A 2024 replication failure on a São Paulo trial is in my source pile but isn't in any Claude critic's response — they all missed it.
  3. The framing privileges one identification strategy when two recent papers used a different approach on similar data and reached different conclusions.

Each of those would have been embarrassing in the final brief.

That's the value. Not that Gemini is smarter on policing. That a different model, reading the same pile, notices a different thing.

Illustrative, not a transcript

The findings above are drawn from the kinds of failure modes mixed-vendor councils surface in real runs — not a single specific transcript. Use it as a pattern, not as a citation.

docs.title: Skill review — the other place I reach for this
docs.text: The other place is reviewing a draft skill, agent, or workflow before it ships. The plan panel (skeptic + pre-mortem + completeness-checker) is where I run most of these. Swap one seat for Codex when there's real code in the picture and Codex catches the engineering stuff Claude waves through — race conditions in shell pipelines, permission-prompt triggers from && chains, error paths that read fine but never fire.

docs.title: The deep research → synthesis → council chain
docs.text:
Three skills, one workflow. Each does one thing.

  1. /deep-research <topic> — dispatches Claude WebSearch, Codex CLI, and Gemini 2.5 Pro CLI in parallel on the same prompt. Three raw reports land in the project folder, indexed in research-archive/INDEX.md for cross-project lookup. ChatGPT Deep Research, Grok, Perplexity, and Gemini's browser Deep Research are available as opt-in paste-loop arms (--tool chatgpt, etc.) — never volunteered as bonus arms.

  2. /dr-synthesize <report-paths...> — combines 2+ raw reports into a single synthesis with a mandatory ## Source Reports block preserving absolute paths to the originals. Surfaces agreements, contradictions, gaps, and per-source unique insights. Synthesis is always a new file; raw inputs are never edited.

  3. /council file:<synthesis-path> --peer gemini — runs the cross-vendor critic pattern this page is about, on the synthesis output, before I trust it.

The chain is: discover sources → run /deep-research → run /dr-synthesize → run /council on the synthesis. Each step writes to disk, so you can stop, inspect, and resume. I rarely run all three in one sitting.

Install pointers: /deep-research and /dr-synthesize in the skill catalog. The full deep-research workflow lives on its own page.

docs.title: Setup: Codex CLI
docs.text:
In Claude, type /kit-setup. It finds Codex — on a Mac, the copy inside the ChatGPT desktop app (Codex merged into it in July 2026, and it isn't put on your PATH); on Windows, OpenAI's Codex command-line tool, which you install first — sends it a test question, and offers the one-time sign-in if it needs one. The full walkthrough, both directions, is covered in Connect another model.

The /codex one-shot command wraps this for ad-hoc use; /council --peer codex uses it for council seats.

docs.title: Setup: Gemini CLI
docs.text:
Install via npm:

npm install -g @google/gemini-cli

Authenticate (OAuth, browser flow):

gemini auth

Pin the Pro model. The OAuth default is the lighter Flash-Lite model, which is not the same critic. Always run with -m gemini-2.5-pro or set it as a default in your shell config:

gemini -m gemini-2.5-pro -p "summarize this in one sentence: continuous integration"

The /gemini one-shot skill pins the Pro model automatically. So does /council --peer gemini.

docs.title: Use them as council critics
docs.text:
/council --peer codex <topic>
/council --peer gemini <topic>

This swaps one Claude critic for a peer-vendor critic, keeping the parallel-dispatch + separate-synthesis structure. Auto-mapping picks the swap target based on which lens the peer is best at:

Peer Best swap target Why Codex skeptic, pre-mortem, harsh-referee Empirical rigor, failure-mode hunting Gemini completeness-checker, domain-expert, academic-editor Long-context synthesis, broad coverage

The swapped seat dispatches as a Bash call to the peer CLI in parallel with the remaining Claude Task calls. The peer's output lands in /tmp/council-peer-<run-id>.md and gets read alongside the Claude critic outputs in the synthesis pass.

Direction matters. Claude → peer only. Do not swap so the peer is the senior critic and Claude is the junior — that's asymmetric dismissal, where the synthesis treats the peer as authoritative without earning it.

If the peer binary is missing, the council prints one line ("Gemini CLI not installed; falling back to all-Claude council") and continues. Graceful degradation, not abort.

docs.title: Use them as one-shot helpers
docs.text:
When you don't need a council — just a single second opinion — the /codex and /gemini skills run a one-shot query against the peer:

/codex Review this regression spec and flag the biggest risk you see.
/gemini Skim this 50K-token literature dump and tell me what's missing.

Use /codex when you want an empirical-engineering second eye on a coding or methods question. Use /gemini when you want long-context synthesis or a different search-grounded perspective.

These are not council substitutes. One peer is one critic — same blind spot risk as one Claude. Reach for /council --peer when the stakes warrant the parallel structure.

docs.title: Manual paste-loop for what isn't CLI'd yet
docs.text:
Two tools I use that do not have stable CLIs I trust for council dispatch:

Tool When How to fold in Grok DeepSearch Discovering new tips and accounts (see /tips-scout) Generate prompt locally, paste into grok.com, forward results to self-email Perplexity Citation-anchored fact lookups Paste the question, copy answer with citations

For these, the integration is procedural: paste in, paste out, file the result. They don't ride in the council parallel-dispatch — but their outputs can be quoted into a Claude critic's prompt the next time around.

ChatGPT Deep Research used to live in this table. It's now an opt-in paste-loop arm inside /deep-research (--tool chatgpt) — the skill emits the prompt, you paste it into ChatGPT, and /deep-research --absorb ingests the report back into the project folder with canonical frontmatter. Same paste-loop mechanics, but the skill handles archiving and indexing instead of you.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
What goes wrong, in order of likelihood:

  • Asymmetric dismissal. A non-Claude critic is louder, more confident, or longer than the Claude critics. The synthesis pass over-weights it as "the outsider's view." Mitigation: keep the swap to one seat. Do not stack two peers; do not let the peer write the synthesis.
  • Vendor outage. A peer CLI hangs or returns an error. The council degrades gracefully — falls back to all-Claude with a one-line note. Don't notice for a week, find out the peer hasn't been firing all month.
  • Auth expiry. Codex or Gemini auth tokens go stale. The CLI returns an error that looks like a regular failure. Re-auth and re-run.
  • Model drift. Gemini OAuth defaults to Flash-Lite if you don't pin Pro. The Pro model is the one I rely on for critique. Always pass -m gemini-2.5-pro or set it as default — never trust the OAuth default to be what you want.
  • Rate-limit surprises. Bursts of council runs in a tight window can hit per-vendor rate limits. The council prints a one-line advisory before parallel dispatch but cannot enforce a real limit from inside Claude Code.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• /council — the council pattern this page extends.
  • Continuous Improvement — the tips pipeline uses Grok via the manual paste-loop and /tips-integrate uses an all-Claude five-persona council. Useful contrast.
  • The council workflow — where one-shot /codex and /gemini sit in the broader loop.

I called in a second opinion!

docs.title: Building Skills
docs.text: Skills are the building blocks of a self-improving Claude Code system. This page covers how to create them from scratch.

docs.title: 1. Notice the Pattern
docs.text:
The best skills come from noticing what you do repeatedly. Pay attention to:

  • Prompts you type out more than twice
  • Multi-step workflows you walk Claude through manually
  • Tasks where you always provide the same context or constraints

docs.title: 2. Do It Manually First
docs.text:
Before formalizing anything, do the task with Claude Code through normal conversation. Do it 3-4 times. Each time, notice:

  • What instructions you give
  • What Claude gets right and wrong
  • What you have to correct or clarify
  • What context you always have to re-provide

docs.title: 3. Write the Skill
docs.text:
Create a .md file with:

# Skill Name

[1-2 sentence description of what this skill does and when to use it]

## Arguments

`$ARGUMENTS` can include:
- [What the user can pass in]

## Instructions

### Step 1: [First action]
[What Claude should do]

### Step 2: [Second action]
[What Claude should do]

### Step 3: [Output]
[What Claude should show the user]

Save to ~/.claude/commands/your-skill.md. Restart Claude Code.

docs.title: 4. Test and Iterate
docs.text:
Run the skill. It won't be right the first time. Common issues:

  • Too verbose — Add constraints: "Keep output under 200 words"
  • Missing context — Add more instructions or @ references
  • Wrong format — Specify exact output structure
  • Doesn't handle edge cases — Add error handling sections

docs.title: 5. Stabilize
docs.text:
Once the skill works reliably:

  • Add a version header (*v1.0 — date — description*)
  • Add argument documentation
  • Add error handling for common failures
  • Test with different inputs

docs.title: Arguments ($ARGUMENTS)
docs.text:
The user's input after the command name. /done quick passes quick as $ARGUMENTS.

Common patterns: 

## Arguments
`$ARGUMENTS` can include:
- *(none)* — default behavior
- `quick` — abbreviated output
- `file:path` — specify a file
- `depth:light/standard/deep` — control thoroughness

docs.title: @ References
docs.text:
Load external files into the skill's context:

## Reference Files
@~/.claude/commands/my-references/style-guide.md
@~/.claude/commands/my-references/voice-rules.md

Use for: - Shared rules across multiple skills - Style guides or voice preferences — see Teaching AI your voice for a complete example - Configuration that changes independently

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Anticipate what goes wrong:

## Error Handling
- **No input provided:** Show usage example and exit
- **File not found:** Report the missing path and suggest alternatives
- **MCP not available:** Explain what's missing and offer to proceed without it

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
Be explicit about what the user sees:

### Output

Display:
| Column 1 | Column 2 |
|----------|----------|
| [data]   | [data]   |

Then ask: "Apply these changes? Or provide feedback to adjust."

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
One skill, one job. A skill that tries to do three things will be fragile and hard to improve. Three focused skills are better.

Match complexity to task. A 5-line skill for formatting a quick note is fine. A 200-line skill for comprehensive plan review is also fine. Don't over-engineer simple tasks or under-specify complex ones.

Default to action. Skills should do something useful with no arguments. Make the zero-argument case the most common workflow.

Fail gracefully. When something goes wrong (missing file, MCP not connected), the skill should explain what happened and suggest a fix — not crash silently.

Version and document. Add a version header and argument documentation. Future-you will thank present-you.

docs.title: Patterns to Steal
docs.text:
These patterns appear in well-designed skills:

Pattern What It Does Example Flags parsing Parse $ARGUMENTS for named flags depth:deep, file:path, quick Phased execution Multi-step with user checkpoints Discover → Plan → Implement Depth calibration Adjust thoroughness based on context Light / Standard / Deep Critic stance Explicitly shift Claude's role "You are now the critic, not the planner" Output templates Fixed format for consistent results Status dashboard, review format Iteration gates Pause for user feedback before continuing "Apply these changes? Or adjust?"

See Patterns for the full catalog.

docs.title: /council — Parallel Critics, Separate Synthesis
docs.text:
Looking for the revised workflow? Start with the new council guide. This reference describes the existing setup; the preview workflow and file contract are being redesigned before the skills are updated.

/council is inspired by — but adapted from — Andrej Karpathy's LLM Council idea: ask several models the same question in parallel, then have one separate pass read their answers as data. I borrowed the shape and changed two things. Karpathy's council is cross-model by default; mine is cross-role by default, with one optional cross-vendor seat for Codex or Gemini. And I forbid debate. Single round, no rebuttals, no majority vote on narrative output — the 2025 conformity-drift literature convinced me round-two was not worth the cost.

The mechanic: parallel dispatch of up to four critics, each with one lens and explicitly told not to balance. A separate model run, with no memory of the critique conversation, reads the raw outputs as input data and ships a verdict plus a punch list. That separation is what stops the council from collapsing into the kind of hedged consensus you get from a single chat thread. I learned this watching a single fresh-context agent rubber-stamp a grant aim that a real referee tore apart two weeks later.

For the longer lineage — Tree of Thoughts, eval-juries, Debate — see Lineage and contribution below.

docs.title: Why bother: never ask just one agent
docs.text:
If you take one habit from this site, take this one. Whenever you're doing something that matters, don't just ask the chatbot. Ask for a council, and then make it criticise its own answer with your corrections in the loop.

Here is my honest sense of the payoff. We haven't run the tests, so treat these as impressions rather than measurements:

How you ask Roughly how happy I am with the answer One question to a chatbot ~60% — usable, generic, a bit confident An agent working on your actual files ~80% — grounded in your material, still unchallenged A council, then recursive self-criticism with your feedback ~95% — the version I'd actually send

The last row is doing most of the work, and the part people skip is the recursion: taking the critique back to the thing being criticised, more than once, with your own judgment included each time. One round of criticism is a second opinion. Several rounds is a different process.

A bonus, not a requirement: if you hold more than one subscription, make one seat cross-vendor — --peer codex or --peer gemini. Different models are genuinely good at different things, and a panel that disagrees with itself is worth more than a panel that agrees. One account is still plenty to start.

docs.title: What ships today
docs.text:
Four critics, two panels, a hard cap of four. That is the whole thing.

Critic Lens skeptic Wishful thinking — which load-bearing claims aren't backed by evidence? pre-mortem Works backward from failure — the top three ways this fails completeness-checker What's missing that a domain expert would expect? chief-of-staff What's the actual decision, and what does saying yes cost you? Panel Critics When Plan skeptic + pre-mortem + completeness-checker Architecture decisions, project plans, anything reversible-but-expensive Decision skeptic + pre-mortem + chief-of-staff Go/no-go calls, hiring, accept/reject

Pick one with --type plan or --type decision, or let keyword inference resolve it from the topic ("plan / design / architecture / workflow" → plan; "should I / decide / go or no-go" → decision). Override the roster with --panel a,b,c.

Paper and grant panels are not built yet

An earlier version of this page advertised paper and grant panels with critics called academic-editor, harsh-referee, methodologist, grant-strategist and funder-officer. Those persona files do not exist, so those panels cannot run — the skill stops with "persona file missing" rather than substituting something worse. If you ask for one, it will say so and offer the plan panel as the closest fit.

They are a real intention, not an abandoned one. Until they ship, a manuscript or proposal gets the plan panel, which is a weaker but honest substitute.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
Trigger Panel Architecture or workflow decision Plan — skeptic and pre-mortem disagree about what the real cost is Hiring call, go/no-go Decision — pre-mortem plus chief-of-staff surface failure modes one reviewer rationalizes away A plan you have already revised twice Plan — by the third revision you have stopped seeing it Grant proposal, manuscript Plan panel, knowingly — the specialist critics aren't built

Council is my default for essentially every task. The numbered walkthrough shows how to start with it, respond to the findings, and revise.

docs.title: How to run it
docs.text:
/council <topic or file:path>
/council file:~/plans/fieldwork-plan.md --type plan
/council "should I take the Bogotá site visit in March" --type decision
/council file:~/plans/plan.md --peer codex

Flags: --panel a,b,c for a custom roster · --n 3 for panel size · --type plan|decision · --peer codex|gemini to swap one seat for another vendor.

docs.title: A council in action
docs.text:
The topic: a plan to run a household survey in three Medellín comunas with a six-week field window.

Panel resolved: --type plan → skeptic + pre-mortem + completeness-checker. Dispatched in parallel, shown verbatim in the synthesis output:

  • Skeptic — "Six weeks" is load-bearing and unevidenced. It appears in the budget and the IRB timeline but no line traces to a measured enumeration rate. What is it derived from?
  • Pre-mortem — Top failure: comuna access is withdrawn in week two and the plan has no substitution rule, so the sample frame silently changes mid-field. Second: enumerator attrition with no bench. Third: the pilot and main wave share instruments, so a pilot fix means re-training.
  • Completeness-checker — No refusal-conversion protocol, no plan for partial households, and nothing on what happens to a comuna that completes early. A reviewer asks about all three.

Synthesis (separate model, fresh context): REVISE. Top three patches: derive the six-week figure from the pilot's actual rate or mark it as an assumption; write the comuna-substitution rule before fieldwork, not during; add a refusal-conversion protocol.

Three critics, one verdict, a punch list. Note that the dissent — the pre-mortem's substitution-rule point — is the one that would actually have broken the study, and only one critic raised it.

docs.title: The rules that make it work
docs.text:
These are not stylistic preferences. Each one is load-bearing.

  • Hard cap of four critics. Beyond four, the synthesis gets noisier, not richer. Ask for more and the skill refuses: "more voices adds noise, not signal."
  • Single round only. No iterative debate. Round-two-and-beyond debate among critics drifts toward conformity — well-documented in the 2025 conformity-drift papers.
  • No majority vote on narrative. The synthesis ranks but does not vote. A unanimous panel can still be wrong; a 1-of-4 dissent on the right point is worth more than three agreements on the wrong frame. The worked example above is exactly that case.
  • Separate synthesis dispatch. The synthesis runs in a fresh context. It reads the raw critic outputs as input data — not as the tail of a conversation it was part of.
  • Persona files exist before dispatch. No silent fallback to a generic agent. If a panel names a persona you don't have, the council aborts and tells you which file is missing. Better to fail loudly than to substitute a worse critic without saying so.
  • A peer critic asks first. Sending your input to Codex or Gemini means sending it to another company. The skill checks for confidential or human-subjects material, and asks before it sends.

docs.title: Writing your own critic
docs.text:
The cap is four, so a fifth persona means replacing one, not adding to the panel.

A persona is one markdown file with YAML frontmatter — name, description, tools — and a body that gives the critic exactly one lens and tells it not to balance. The four that ship are the reference: read skeptic.md for the shortest, chief-of-staff.md for the one with the most judgment in it.

Drop yours next to them in the plugin's agents/ directory, then call it:

/council file:~/plans/plan.md --panel skeptic,pre-mortem,your-critic

The single most important line in a persona file is the instruction not to be balanced. A critic told to "give a fair assessment" writes the same hedged paragraph every other critic writes, and the synthesis has nothing to rank.

docs.title: When to add a peer critic
docs.text:
A council of four Claudes still shares one model's blind spots. The fix is to swap one seat for Codex or Gemini — same prompt, different vendor, dispatched in the same parallel call. I have caught failures this way that no all-Claude panel surfaced, mostly around empirical claims Claude wanted to believe.

Setup, flags, and the manual paste-loop for tools without CLIs (Grok, ChatGPT Deep Research, Perplexity) live on the AI integration page.

docs.title: Lineage and contribution
docs.text:
Andrej Karpathy gave the pattern its handle in his "LLM councils" note: parallel critics, separate synthesis, no debate. The lineage is older. The structural shape — multiple draws, evaluate the spread — is the same one Yao et al. (Tree of Thoughts, 2023) used inside a single model's reasoning, and the same one Anthropic's eval-jury work uses for benchmarking. OpenAI's "AI Safety via Debate" sits as the deliberate contrast: I do not allow debate, because the 2025 multi-agent literature on conformity drift convinced me single-round was not negotiable.

My contribution is two narrower things. First, a fixed-persona spin-up — the five-critic tips council, with each persona tuned for one failure mode (catalog conflict, maintenance tax, compounder, first-run, skeptic) and explicitly told not to balance. Second, the cross-vendor swap: one seat goes to Codex or Gemini, dispatched in the same parallel call. Both ship as code, not as theory.

docs.title: Install and setup
docs.text:
/council ships in the starter kit, so if you installed that, you already have it — the Occasional checklist covers it, and there is nothing further to do. The four persona files come with the plugin.

To check it is live, run /council with no arguments in a session: it should ask what you want reviewed rather than reporting an unknown command.

Prefer individual files, or want to see what each one does before installing? See the skill reference.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deep Research — the gather-and-synthesize workflow that produces the kind of input most worth running a council on.
  • Continuous Improvement — the worked tips-pipeline specialization where five fixed personas (catalog conflict, maintenance tax, compounder, first-run, skeptic) decide what enters my CLAUDE.md. The general pattern, applied to one specific domain — and it predates the four-critic cap in the shipped skill.
  • AI integration — cross-vendor critics (Codex, Gemini) as council members; setup, flags, manual paste-loop for tools without CLIs.
  • Fresh-chat review — a manual route when independent agents are unavailable.
  • The council workflow — where /council fits in the broader loop.

docs.title: Research tools I use
docs.text:
An agent is good at working on files you already have. These are good at the step before that: getting research material into a form it can work on.

None is required. Each one removes a specific kind of friction.

The two tools I'd add before either of these — dictation and meeting transcription — now have their own pages in Start Here: Dictate and Transcribe.

As of October 2026.

docs.title: A research notebook — NotebookLM
docs.text:
Upload a stack of papers and ask questions across all of them at once. It is strongest where agents are weakest: a very large pile of source documents that you want to interrogate rather than edit.

Gemini Notebook

docs.title: A reference manager — Zotero
docs.text:
Free, and the standard in most research fields. It holds your citations and PDFs in one library with a consistent structure, which matters here for one reason: a well-kept Zotero library is a folder of PDFs with real metadata, and that is exactly the kind of input an agent handles well.

You can also connect it directly, so the agent can search your library rather than you exporting from it. That route is a connector, not something built into the app:

Connect your apps

Zotero doesn't have its own page here yet

The connection route is covered on the Connect your apps page, but there is no Zotero walkthrough on this site. Treat the paragraph above as the summary, not the instructions.

docs.title: What I'd skip at the start
docs.text:
Adding tools is the easiest way to feel productive without being productive. Each one is another subscription, another place your data lives, and another thing to keep working.

The honest order: get an agent working on a real folder first. Add dictation when typing starts feeling like the bottleneck. Add the others when a specific task keeps failing for want of them — not before.

What this costs

I tried one of these!

docs.title: Connect your apps
docs.text:
By default the agent can only see the folder you point it at. Connecting an app widens that: it can read your email, search your documents, check your calendar.

There are two routes. Most people only need the first one, which takes a few minutes and no terminal. The second is older, more capable, and considerably more work.

Connectors MCP servers Set up where A page in your Claude account Your computer, by hand Terminal needed No Yes Time ~5 minutes per service 10–60 minutes per service Covers Mail, calendar, documents — the common services Zotero, Apple apps, WhatsApp, anything niche Breaks when Rarely A repo goes unmaintained, a token expires, a path changes

Start at Connectors. Only read MCP servers if what you need isn't in the directory.

As of October 2026. Both routes change often — where this page and the app disagree, the app is right.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text: A connector is a service Anthropic has already wired up. You switch it on once in your Claude account and it shows up in your sessions.

docs.title: Turning one on
docs.text:
1. Go to claude.ai/customize/connectors. This is a page in your Claude account, not a setting inside the desktop app — a common place to get stuck.
  2. Browse claude.ai/directory for what's available. Gmail, Microsoft 365 and Google Calendar are all there.
  3. Connect the one you want and complete the sign-in it asks for. This is the normal provider window — Google's or Microsoft's own.
  4. Start a new session. The desktop app hands your connectors to each local session automatically; there is nothing to configure on this end.

Two things that stop this working

On a Team or Enterprise plan, only an administrator can add connectors. If you are on a university or company account and the Connectors page won't let you add anything, that is why — ask whoever administers your Claude account. This affects a lot of academic readers.

Connectors need a Claude subscription login. They do not load if you are signed in with an API key or routed through a third-party provider.

docs.title: Before you connect anything
docs.text:
A connector gives the agent your whole account for that service — not a folder or a label. The mail connector can read any message; the drive connector can reach any file; the calendar connector sees private events. There is no way to narrow it to a subset.

If you never want the agent sending mail on your behalf, set that tool to Blocked, not "needs approval." Blocked removes the tool before Claude ever sees it; approval prompts can be answered in a hurry. On the desktop app in particular, Blocked is the setting that reliably holds.

For a service holding data you would not want processed by an AI, don't connect it. For something seasonal — tax documents, say — connect it while you need it and disconnect afterwards. The tax workflow privacy guide walks through that pattern, and Privacy covers how data moves through these tools generally.

docs.title: Services this page does not cover
docs.text:
The directory is the live list and it changes; this page does not duplicate it. OneDrive, Outlook and Slack have no per-service instructions here. Outlook and OneDrive may be covered by the Microsoft 365 connector — check the directory. If a service you need isn't there, the MCP route below is the fallback.

I connected something.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
MCP is the older route. It reaches things connectors don't, and it costs real time. Everything below needs a terminal.

Before you start down this road

Gmail, Microsoft 365 and Google Calendar cannot do local sign-in from Claude Code. That is exactly why the Google route below takes 45 minutes and a Google Cloud project — you are building what the connector already provides. If the connector works for you, it is strictly the better option.

You don't need any of this to get value from the app. It reads and edits files, drafts, reviews plans and captures notes with nothing connected. The first-session skills all work without it.

docs.title: How the configuration works
docs.text:
MCP servers live in ~/.claude.json, which Claude reads at startup. Each entry names a command to run plus any credentials it needs. You edit that file by hand.

Getting an error? Ask Claude.

Paste the error straight into the message box — I'm getting an error trying to connect. Here's what I see: [paste the error]. It can usually diagnose a configuration problem on the spot.

docs.title: Google Workspace
docs.text:
⏱ 45–60 min Hardest thing on this page

Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar, Drive and Tasks from one server. Repository: taylorwilsdon/google_workspace_mcp

Needs: Python 3.10+, uv, and a free Google Cloud Console account.

1. Install uv: 

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

2. Clone and install: 

cd ~
git clone https://github.com/taylorwilsdon/google_workspace_mcp
cd google_workspace_mcp
uv sync

3. Create Google OAuth credentials. The involved part — you are creating your own project in Google Cloud Console.

  1. Go to console.cloud.google.com and create a project
  2. Enable each API you want, from the API Library: Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Calendar, Tasks
  3. Credentials → Create Credentials → OAuth client ID, application type Desktop app
  4. Download the client ID and secret
  5. Switch the project to Production. Under Google Auth platform → Audience, change "Testing" to "Production". In Testing mode tokens expire after 7 days and you re-authenticate weekly. This is the single most common complaint about this setup, and it takes one click now versus every week forever.

4. Add it to ~/.claude.json under mcpServers:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "google_workspace": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "/path/to/uv",
      "args": [
        "run", "--directory", "/path/to/google_workspace_mcp",
        "main.py", "--tools", "drive", "docs", "sheets", "gmail", "calendar", "tasks"
      ],
      "env": {
        "GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID": "your-client-id.apps.googleusercontent.com",
        "GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET": "your-client-secret",
        "OAUTHLIB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT": "1",
        "USER_GOOGLE_EMAIL": "your-email@gmail.com"
      }
    }
  }
}

Replace the paths and credentials. which uv gives you the first one. OAUTHLIB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT permits OAuth over HTTP on localhost, which is standard for a desktop app talking only to your own machine — never set it on a real server.

5. Restart and test with Search my Gmail for emails from last week.

Limitations: can't create Google Doc tabs; no suggesting mode or track changes; uses roughly 26K tokens of context for all tools. Trim the --tools list if you run short.

docs.title: WhatsApp
docs.text:
⏱ 15 min

Read messages and search history. Search GitHub for whatsapp-mcp — several implementations exist and they vary. Clone one, npm install, run it once to get a QR code, scan that with your phone, then add it to ~/.claude.json.

Expect friction: the session drops whenever your laptop sleeps and you re-scan the QR code. Chat metadata goes stale, so fetch messages directly rather than trusting a chat list.

docs.title: Zotero
docs.text:
⏱ 10 min Easiest one here

Search your library and pull citations. Package: mcp-zotero (npm). Get an API key and your user ID from zotero.org/settings/keys, then:

"zotero": {
  "type": "stdio",
  "command": "npx",
  "args": ["mcp-zotero"],
  "env": {
    "ZOTERO_API_KEY": "your-api-key",
    "ZOTERO_USER_ID": "your-user-id"
  }
}

docs.title: Apple apps (Mac only)
docs.text:
⏱ 10 min

Notes, Calendar, Contacts, Reminders, Messages and Mail through the native apps.

Mostly broken, and unmaintained

apple-mcp is archived. Reminders (create and read), Calendar (read) and Contacts (read) work reasonably. Notes is broken — use apple-notes-mcp. Mail is inconsistent — use the mail connector. Messages is limited. Apple has announced native MCP support in a future macOS release, which will replace this entirely. Check the issue tracker before spending time here.

Runs via Bun — curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash — then:

"apple-mcp": {
  "type": "stdio",
  "command": "/path/to/.bun/bin/bunx",
  "args": ["--no-cache", "apple-mcp@latest"],
  "env": {}
}

docs.title: Granola
docs.text:
⏱ 15 min

Granola now publishes an official connector for Claude and ChatGPT — switch it on like any other connector and search "Granola". It returns meeting notes on every plan and full verbatim transcripts on paid plans (Business and up); the free plan gets notes only. Checked 19 October 2026.

This replaces the older community server, which returned summaries only. For how to get transcripts into a project folder and what to do with them, see Transcribe every meeting.

docs.title: Slack and Microsoft Teams
docs.text: Servers exist on GitHub but vary in quality and maintenance, and some need an Enterprise plan. The setup pattern is the same as above — clone, configure, restart — so the work is in picking a well-maintained one. Check recent commits and open issues before you start. Check the connector directory first; a supported connector beats an unmaintained server.

docs.title: Using more than one computer
docs.text:
Syncs via your cloud folder: CLAUDE.md, your skills folder, and the MCP configuration itself.

Stays local to each machine: OAuth tokens (authenticate once per machine), the server repositories (clone on each), and ~/.claude.json.

Setting up a second machine: clone the repositories, copy your configuration in, fix the paths to match, restart. First use prompts for authentication.

Connectors need none of this — they follow your account.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Fix A connector won't add Team or Enterprise plan — only an admin can. Also check you're signed in with a Claude subscription, not an API key Google auth expired Delete the credentials file in the server folder (usually ~/.google_workspace_mcp/credentials/) and re-authenticate. If it keeps happening weekly, the project is still in Testing mode — switch it to Production WhatsApp session dropped Re-run the server and scan the QR code again. Expected after sleep Server not responding Run the command manually in a terminal; confirm every path in ~/.claude.json is absolute; restart Running out of context claude doctor shows MCP tool context usage. Disable unused servers or trim --tools

Shared computers

Anyone who can open a terminal on your machine can run claude and reach every connected service, with no further login. On a shared machine, use separate user accounts, or remove the entries from ~/.claude.json when you're done. Conversation history also sits in ~/.claude/ and can contain content from connected services.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
The skill reference — the workflows that use these connections.

That's everything I need connected for now.

docs.title: Picking your agent
docs.text:
Two companies make the kind of agent this site is about: Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex. Both sit on your desktop (apps like any other), read the files in a folder you point them at, and change them while you watch. Either will run every workflow here. The choice matters much less than people expect, and it is reversible — so make it once, quickly, and move on.

The truth is, I pay for and use both daily. A supercharged user should eventually use both, but for now, the choice is not big.

docs.title: The short answer
docs.text:
One question settles it: do you already pay for Claude? Does your company?

  • Already pay for Claude (Pro or above, about $20/month) → use Claude.
  • Don't → use Codex from OpenAI.

That is the whole rule. If you already pay for ChatGPT and not Claude, invert it. If you pay for neither, Codex is the usual recommendation — it's my current preferred app, and you can try small tasks with Codex before paying.

Nothing you learn on one is wasted if you later move to the other — the workflows on this site are the same either way, and the starter kit has a route for both. What does differ is the price of entry and how much friction you hit installing things, which is what the table below is for.

docs.title: Claude Code vs Codex
docs.text:
Start with what doesn't change. Both apps put an agent in front of your own files, both will read a folder and edit what is in it, and neither is better at the actual work. Claims that one is categorically smarter rarely survive contact with a real task.

What does change, and changes often, is the user interaction and capabilities in each app.

Claude Codex Where to get it claude.com/download macOS · Windows What the app is called Claude desktop app; agentic work lives in the Code tab Now part of the ChatGPT desktop app – Codex is one tab Plan needed Code tab requires a paid plan (Pro at $17/mo or above). Chat works on Free. Listed as included on the Free plan, but free use is local-only with tight limits and no option to buy credits. Plus ($20/mo) is the practical floor.

docs.title: Pros of choosing Codex
docs.text:
Deep Research. The single best reason to have a ChatGPT subscription. Give it a question and it spends 5-30 minutes searching the web, synthesizing multiple sources, and producing a structured report with citations. Claude can do web searches, but they're shallow by comparison. The free ChatGPT plan gives you access to a small number of deep research requests per month, but paying for Codex simultaneously buys you extra deep research requests each month – like a two for one plan.

Annotating. You can open files direclty inside the app, highlight sentences and request changes. Send all your comments at once.

docs.title: Pros of choosing Claude
docs.text:
Everything in the Code tab. The desktop app that reads your files, manages your email, and runs custom skills has no real ChatGPT equivalent. If you use Claude Code, Claude is your primary AI tool by default.

Long-form writing and editing. Claude consistently produces better prose — maintaining voice, following structural instructions, and providing substantive feedback.

Complex reasoning. For research design, methodology review, and strategic planning, Claude Opus 4.6 tends to produce more thoughtful output than GPT-4o.

Projects and persistent context. Claude.ai's Projects feature lets you create a workspace with instructions and files that persist across conversations — better than ChatGPT's memory system for structured, project-based work.

docs.title: The bottom line
docs.text:
If you can only pick one: Claude, especially if you plan to use Claude Code.

If you can afford both: Use Claude as your primary tool and ChatGPT for Deep Research and web-heavy tasks. They're genuinely complementary.

If you're just starting: Start with whichever one you already have, then run your first session — the ten steps there work the same on both.

For a detailed decision framework covering Claude Code, Claude.ai, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, see the Tool Limitations & When to Use What guide.

I've picked my agent!

docs.title: AI Project Folders: Turn Any Recurring Task into a System
docs.text:
No Claude Code required

Ready to build? Skip to the setup. Want to see examples first? Jump to the examples.

A single file stores your stable preferences, hard constraints, and behavioral rules for a recurring domain. Every new conversation starts from that file instead of from scratch.

I use project folders for two things: life (travel, shopping, health) and work (research writing, proposals, course prep). The pattern is the same — I'll walk through it using family travel as the main example, then show how it applies across domains.

This works in both ChatGPT Projects and Claude.ai Projects, with minor setup differences noted below.

docs.title: What This Actually Looks Like
docs.text:
Before you invest time reading, here's the payoff in 30 seconds.

Without a project file — you ask ChatGPT to help plan a summer trip:

Here are my top 10 recommendations for a family summer vacation:

1. Yellowstone National Park — stunning geysers and wildlife 2. San Diego — beautiful beaches and the famous zoo 3. Orlando — Walt Disney World and Universal Studios 4. Maui — tropical paradise with snorkeling and hiking 5. Washington D.C. — free museums and monuments...

Generic. Tourist-list. Could be for any family on Earth.

With a project file — same question, same chatbot:

Given your preference for high-altitude or desert climates in summer, your teen daughter's horse-riding priority, and your budget for HomeExchange accommodations, I'd suggest looking at three options in the Mountain West. Note: I'm flagging that two of these will exceed 85°F in late July, which historically has limited your outdoor climbing days. Here's a comparison with trade-offs for each family member...

It references your specific constraints without you repeating them. That's the difference.

A project file is just a well-written prompt you write once and reuse forever.

I built my first project file for family vacation planning. That one file — and the failures that shaped it — taught me the pattern I now use for everything. See the examples below.

docs.title: Build Your First File
docs.text:
This takes about an hour for a first file, then 10 minutes to update after each use.

But before you keep reading — open ChatGPT or Claude in another tab and think of one domain where you keep repeating yourself to the AI. Vacations, shopping, meal planning, a type of professional writing. Just pick one. That's what you'll build.

docs.title: Platform setup
docs.text:
• ChatGPT: Create a project from the sidebar. Add standing instructions in the project's settings and reference files as sources. Current project controls.
  • Claude.ai: Open Projects, create a project, and use Set project instructions. Add reference files to project knowledge. Current project controls.

Use the project features available in your account and workspace. If projects aren't available, keep your context in a text file and paste it into each new chat.

Start with rules and preferences in instructions. Add files when the task needs more detailed reference material, such as past itineraries or tables of data. Keep important decisions explicitly in those sources rather than assuming every new chat will remember them.

docs.title: Step 1: Narrate your situation
docs.text:
Open a new conversation and dump everything you know about this domain. Be messy. Be thorough. Don't organize — just talk. Even three sentences is enough to start — the interview in Step 2 will fill the gaps.

Here's the difference between a thin dump and a useful one:

Too thin: "I like beaches and good food."

Useful: "We travel as a family of four — the kids need activity, not scenery. My partner is pescatarian. I'm a rock climber. We hate tourist traps, we avoid extreme heat, and our last three trips that worked were a mountain town in the Pacific Northwest, a cultural city in southern Mexico, and a desert trip in winter. The beach resort we tried was a disaster."

More detail = better file. Include what went wrong on past attempts, not just what went right.

docs.title: Step 2: Ask the AI to interview you
docs.text:
After your dump, paste this prompt:

Based on what I've shared, interview me to fill in the gaps. Ask me
12 questions, one at a time, covering:

1. Who is involved and what are each person's individual preferences?
2. What does each person actively dislike or avoid?
3. What are our hard constraints (budget ceilings, date windows, health limits)?
4. What specific thresholds matter (temperature ranges, drive times, flight durations)?
5. What past experiences worked well — and what specific conditions made them work?
6. What past experiences failed — and what went wrong?
7. What's our typical logistics setup (car rental, accommodation style, pace)?
8. What trade-offs are we usually willing to make?
9. What trade-offs are we NOT willing to make?
10. Are there any behavioral instructions for you — things I want you to always
    do or never do when helping with this domain?
11. What patterns have I noticed across my best experiences?
12. Is there anything I mentioned that seems contradictory or that you want
    to clarify?

Ask one question at a time. Wait for my answer before moving to the next.

Answer honestly. The AI is building a model of your preferences — the more specific you are, the better your file will be.

Add 'avoids' per person, not just 'likes'

Avoidances are the true constraints. A family member who "likes beaches" is flexible. A family member who "refuses to hike uphill for more than 30 minutes" is a hard constraint that changes every recommendation.

Use explicit threshold numbers

"Flag anything over 85°F" works. "We don't like heat" doesn't. "Budget under $300/night for accommodation" works. "We're not extravagant" doesn't. Numbers give the AI something to actually check against.

Checkpoint: You should now have 10-15 specific answers. If you have fewer than 8, go back — the thin ones are usually avoids and thresholds.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask the AI to produce a canonical file
docs.text:
After the interview, paste this prompt:

Now synthesize everything — my initial dump and all my interview answers — into
a single canonical project file. Follow these rules:

1. SEPARATE stable preferences from situation-specific details. The file should
   contain only things that are true across all future uses of this domain.
   Anything specific to one instance (a particular trip, a specific purchase)
   should be excluded.

2. USE EXPLICIT THRESHOLD NUMBERS, not adjectives. "Prefer daytime highs
   65-80°F; flag anything over 85°F" not "we like mild weather."

3. ORGANIZE BY CATEGORY: People/preferences, Constraints, Logistics,
   Evidence from past experience, Behavioral instructions for you.

4. GIVE EACH PERSON THEIR OWN SECTION with both preferences AND explicit
   avoids.

5. FLAG anything you inferred versus what I stated directly, so I can
   correct inferences.

6. KEEP IT UNDER 500 WORDS. Shorter files produce better adherence.
   Aim for 300-500 words.

Format as clean markdown. This file will be pasted into a ChatGPT or
Claude project as standing instructions.

Checkpoint: Your file should be 300-500 words with at least one threshold number and one "avoids" entry per person or category. If it's over 600 words, ask the AI to prune situation-specific details.

docs.title: Starter template
docs.text:
If you'd rather start from a template and fill it in, here's a generic one that works for any recurring domain:

# [DOMAIN] Planning Context

## Key Instructions
- [BEHAVIORAL RULE: e.g., "Be analytical, not agreeable. Offer critical opinions."]
- [BEHAVIORAL RULE: e.g., "Always flag potential problems before I ask."]
- [BEHAVIORAL RULE: e.g., "Provide 1.5-2x more options than needed so I can choose."]

## People & Preferences
### [Person 1]
- Priorities: [what they care about most]
- Also enjoys: [secondary interests]
- Avoids: [explicit dislikes — be specific]

### [Person 2]
- Priorities: [...]
- Avoids: [...]

## Hard Constraints
- Budget: [specific ceiling, e.g., "under $300/night accommodation, $150/day activities"]
- Time windows: [when this typically happens]
- [Other constraint]: [with threshold number]
- [Other constraint]: [with threshold number]

## Logistics & Preferences
- [How you typically handle logistics in this domain]
- [Pace/style preferences]

## Evidence: What's Worked
- [Past experience that worked] — conditions: [why it worked]
- [Past experience that worked] — conditions: [why it worked]

## Evidence: What Hasn't Worked
- [Past experience that failed] — problem: [what went wrong]
- [Past experience that failed] — problem: [what went wrong]

## Key Success Factors
- [Factor 1]
- [Factor 2]
- [Factor 3]

Good fill-in: Budget: under $300/night for accommodation, $150/day activities

Bad fill-in: Budget: moderate

The bad version gives the AI nothing to work with. The good version gives it a number to check against.

docs.title: How to know it's working
docs.text:
You're done when your file has: stable preferences for each person, at least 2-3 explicit constraints with threshold numbers, and an "avoids" section.

Test it: Start a completely new conversation in the project (this tests whether the file actually loaded, not whether it's in your current context). Ask for three suggestions in your domain. The hard test: at least one option should be explicitly eliminated or flagged because it violates a constraint in your file. If all three options look generically good, the file isn't specific enough — go back to the avoids and thresholds.

docs.title: When it doesn't work
docs.text:
AI ignores the file. This happens occasionally, especially in long conversations. Reprompt: "Reference my project file directly. Do not give generic recommendations." Starting a fresh conversation usually fixes it.

Generic tourist-list results. Your file lacks specificity. The fix is almost always the same: add explicit avoids, threshold numbers, and past experience patterns. The AI defaults to generic when it doesn't have enough constraints to differentiate.

File too long or bloated. Prune to under 500 words. Remove situation-specific details (those belong in per-instance briefs, not the canonical file). Shorter files produce noticeably better adherence, especially in ChatGPT. Aim for 300-500 words after stabilization.

docs.title: How This Actually Develops
docs.text:
Don't expect your file to be good on day one. It follows a predictable arc:

Stage 1: Messy dump → first usable file (conversations 1-2). Your file is rough. You update it substantially after every use. The AI's output is better than no-context conversations but still occasionally generic.

Stage 2: Failure modes teach you the rules (conversations 3-5). You discover what's missing — avoids, thresholds, evidence patterns — usually because the AI recommended something that violated an unstated constraint. These failures are the most productive part of the process. Each one adds a specific rule to your file.

Stage 3: Maintenance, not building (conversation 6+). The file is reliable enough to trust. Updates are 1-2 lines after each use, not rewrites. Your job shifts from building the file to pruning it — removing anything situation-specific that crept in, keeping it under 500 words.

docs.title: See It in Action
docs.text:
The domain changes. The structure doesn't. Three examples — from simple to detailed.

Health & FitnessVacation PlanningShopping Decisions

A research and consultation folder — uploaded files for detailed health context.

This isn't a planning folder like vacation or shopping. It's a research and consultation folder. I keep a detailed markdown file with my health baseline, labs, medications, and training patterns. When I have a question — blood pressure trends, a sports injury, nutrition claims, physical therapy options — the AI gives advice that accounts for my full context instead of starting from scratch.

How I actually use this

I use this folder in a few different modes:

  • Deep thinking sessions — extended conversations where I work through a specific health question. Understanding a lab result trend, evaluating treatment options for an injury, figuring out how to modify training around a constraint.
  • Deep research reports — when I want to understand claims about nutrition, blood pressure management, or physical therapy approaches. I ask for evidence with primary sources. I'm comfortable reading the actual studies, so I ask the AI to be skeptical of small-sample or non-experimental research.
  • Quick consultations — minor ailments, aches and pains, equipment recommendations, whether a new monitoring device would be useful.

Dr. Claude and Dr. ChatGPT are both genuinely good at this. I generally trust ChatGPT most for deep research in this domain — its web browsing lets it pull current studies and reviews. Claude tends to be better for structured analysis when I already have the information.

The key insight: none of this works well without the profile file. Without it, you get generic advice for a generic person. With it, you get advice calibrated to your age, your medications, your injury history, and your actual training goals.

What goes in the profile: A single markdown document with your stable health context — core baseline (age range, weight range, blood pressure trend), medications & supplements (the most important section for safety — the AI cross-references interactions), medical history & injuries (written in functional terms like "no deep flexion beyond 90°"), lifestyle & activity pattern, family history, monitoring devices, and preferences & constraints.

The instructions file (separate from the profile) tells the AI how to behave:

## Standing preferences
- Base guidance on evidence and cite primary sources
- Be skeptical of small-sample or non-experimental research
- Flag anything requiring clinician approval
- Focus on performance and injury prevention, not generic weight-loss tips

## How to use the profile
- Load or reference the master health profile at the start of any thread
- If information seems out of date, ask before guessing

## Privacy
- No full identifiers in outputs
- Keep advice general enough to be safe if seen by others

Files vs. instructions only: This is a domain where uploaded files matter. Your health profile has tables of data — baseline vitals, medication lists, training patterns — that are too detailed for the instructions field alone. Upload the profile as a source file (ChatGPT) or project knowledge (Claude.ai), and keep the behavioral rules in instructions. Compare this to shopping, where the instructions file alone is enough.

Building your own: Use the same three-step process from the setup guide above. Privacy note: use ranges instead of exact values. Keep detailed lab results in conversation, not in the permanent file. By the fifth or sixth session, the file stabilizes and updates become a line or two after each doctor's visit or training shift.

The original folder — family travel with constraints, thresholds, and an evidence bank.

The first file I built wasn't for research. It was for planning family vacations. That sounds trivial, but it taught me the pattern I now use for everything. We once planned a trip to a great spot for climbing and rafting. Turned out it was one of the hotter times of year — we lost several outdoor days. That failure is what taught me to add explicit temperature thresholds instead of vague preferences like "we don't like heat."

The full story: how a messy dump became a system

It started as a brain dump. My wife and I were planning a summer trip and I pasted a wall of text into ChatGPT — where we'd been, what the kids liked, what we couldn't stand. The AI gave decent suggestions but kept recommending beach resorts, which isn't us.

So I refined the dump. Added explicit "avoids" for each family member. Added temperature thresholds instead of "we prefer mild weather." Added past trip patterns — not just where we went, but which conditions made them work: high altitude, desert-like, culturally rich small towns.

By the third or fourth trip planned this way, the file had stabilized. I wasn't rewriting it anymore — just adding a line or two after each trip. After about six conversations, the file was reliable enough to trust. New trip planning conversations started producing useful, specific suggestions on the first exchange.

System instructions — the behavioral rules that prevent generic output:

I want you to be an unusually investigative advisor for travel.
Instead of focusing on being highly agreeable, be analytical and
offer critical opinions where appropriate.

When starting a new discussion, analyze the prompt and come back with:
* What kind of vacation we want
* Who is going (if not clear)
* Major red flags based on my preferences
* Potential travel restrictions

Please do not hallucinate details but investigate and confirm
wherever possible.

Why "unusually investigative"? Without this, the AI defaults to agreeable mode — it recommends whatever you seem excited about. "Major red flags" forces it to cross-reference your preferences before generating suggestions.

Persona preferences — each family member gets their own section:

### Teen Daughter
- Passions: Animals (especially horses — horseback riding is her top priority),
  water sports, reading, bookstores, shopping
- Avoids: Steady uphill hikes (unless scrambly or leading to water),
  heavy insect areas, long drives without stops

The design pattern: preferences tell the AI what to suggest. Avoids tell it what to filter out.

Logistics constraints — every constraint has a number:

## Climate & Weather Requirements
- Temperature: Prefer daytime highs 65-80°F; flag anything over 85°F
- Humidity: Low humidity preferred, especially if over 80°F

## Travel Logistics
- Base strategy: Prefer one home base for 5-7 days with activities
  within 75-minute drives
- Driving limits: Maximum 8 hours/day, preferably 4
- Accommodation: Heavy users of home exchange

Not "we don't like long drives" but "maximum 8 hours, preferably 4." Not "mild weather" but "65-80°F, flag over 85°F."

Evidence bank — tag each entry with its conditions:

## Successful Past Patterns
- Mountain/high altitude — Pacific Northwest in summer
  (worked: climate, outdoor sports, uncrowded)
- Cultural/authentic — Southern Mexico
  (worked: food scene, local flavor, affordable, kids engaged)

## Good but Imperfect
- Coastal Mexico resort town (too muggy; inland towns were better)
- Major European cities in summer (too crowded; rural areas excellent)

This is the most powerful section — it gives the AI pattern-matching data instead of just preference lists.

How a trip actually works: Start a new conversation with a short trip brief (dates, who's going, special constraints). The canonical file provides everything else. Review the AI's initial response — did it reference your constraints? Ask for 1.5-2x the options you need with explicit trade-offs. Pick 1-2 top options and build the itinerary. After the trip, add 1-2 stable learnings.

Instructions-only folder — durability over price, curated shortlists, and a system that learns from every purchase.

I built my first shopping file after the third time I asked ChatGPT for a product recommendation and got a wall of options with no clear winner. The AI kept recommending unknown brands, inventing prices, and ignoring that I care more about durability than saving $20.

The full story: how ad hoc prompting became a system

The first failure mode I noticed: it didn't remember that I value durability over marginal savings. Every new conversation, I'd re-explain my decision style from scratch. The second: it would recommend 15 options when I needed 3. The third: it sounded certain about things it couldn't possibly know — stock levels, sale prices, review consensus.

The real shift came when I separated how I decide from what I'm buying now. My decision criteria don't change between purchases. So I pulled them into a canonical file. The per-purchase details go into a brief I paste fresh each time.

Decision posture:

- Prioritize best-in-class or best value-for-money products.
  Mention budget options when durability is less critical.
- Avoid unknown or low-quality brands, especially random
  marketplace imports. Favor well-known, trusted brands.
- Value durability and long-term satisfaction over first
  impressions. Highlight reviews reflecting long-term use.

Without the first line, the AI optimizes for price — the wrong objective. Without the second, it recommends cheap imports with inflated reviews. Without the third, it weights "just arrived" praise over long-term ownership reports.

How to recommend:

- Provide curated shortlists (3-5 picks), side-by-side
  comparisons, and pros/cons summaries.
- Include links to expert reviews (e.g., Wirecutter, Outdoor
  Gear Lab). I like to read the deep dives myself.
- Do not recommend subscription or auto-renewal options
  unless explicitly requested.

Run brief template:

Item: Standing desk for home office
Use case: Daily use, 8+ hours. Alternate sitting/standing.

Must-haves:
- Stable at standing height (no wobble during typing)
- Fits 2 monitors + laptop
- Quiet motor

Constraints:
- Budget: under $700
- Width: max 60 inches (alcove)
- Timeline: no rush, can wait for a sale

Avoid: particle board tops, brands without long-term reviews

Notice what's not in the brief: how I evaluate products, my review-reading heuristics, my preference for durability over price. All of that lives in the instructions file.

Structured output — the AI produces a consistent format every time: shortlist (3-5 picks, labeled), comparison table, who each pick is for, failure modes, buy path, and questions (only if truly needed).

Common failure modes and fixes:

Failure Fix in the file Too many options Shortlist cap (3-5) + forced tradeoffs Junk brands Default to reputable; require opt-in for risk Invented facts "Unknown unless provided"; label uncertainty File bloat Stable-only rule + size limit + quarterly prune

docs.title: Work
docs.text:
The same principles apply to professional workflows — writing, proposals, reports, literature reviews.

ChatGPT Deep Research deserves a special mention: it may be the single most valuable AI tool for faculty right now. Give it a clear, well-engineered prompt and it produces detailed research briefings that would take hours of manual searching.

For project management workflows that go beyond project folders — weekly reviews, living dashboards, automated proposal drafting — see the Project Management section.

docs.title: Choose the tool available to you
docs.text:
This pattern works in either chatbot: keep reusable instructions, supply the relevant sources, and give each new task a clear brief. Use the tool available to you, then compare another if the result isn't meeting your needs. Search, research, and file features depend on your account and settings.

When a task depends on current prices, opening hours, or availability, use current sources and verify the details before committing. Having a browser or a good project file doesn't make those facts automatically reliable.

What I Wish I'd Known

  • Start with a messy dump, not a template. Your first version will be bad. That's the process. The template above is a finishing structure, not a starting point.
  • Improve it through use. Add what the first few attempts reveal, then keep checking it as your needs change. A familiar file can still contain stale or mistaken information.
  • Post-use updates should be 1-2 lines, not essays. One new rule. One updated threshold. One "this worked under these conditions."
  • Guard against the AI being too agreeable. Specific techniques: ask it to steelman the option it's not recommending. Ask it to identify which of your constraints a proposed option violates. Ask it to generate one "bad fit" option alongside good ones so you can see the contrast.
  • If you edit the canonical file mid-conversation, start a new conversation afterward. The AI has already processed the old version and may produce inconsistent results mixing old and new instructions.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Level up your prompts

    The prompting techniques that make project files (and everything else) work better.

    Getting better answers

  • Understand the landscape

    When to use ChatGPT vs Claude — and when it matters for project folders.

    ChatGPT vs Claude

  • Go deeper

    When project folders aren't enough, Claude Code turns recurring tasks into automated workflows.

    Get Started

My folders make some semblance of sense now.

docs.title: Set up rules and guidelines
docs.text:
Your instruction file says who you are and where things live. Rules are the other half: what to do, and what never to do. They apply to everything, so you write them once instead of repeating yourself every session.

The difference matters. "My drafts live in ~/Projects" is context. "Never send an email without showing me the draft first" is a rule.

docs.title: Start with the ones you've already repeated
docs.text:
Don't sit down to write a rulebook. Watch for the moment you correct the agent twice for the same thing — that correction is your first rule. Mine came from being irritated, not from planning:

  • Meeting notes go at the top of the file, newest first.
  • Never create a mail filter without asking. Filters run when I'm not there.
  • Drafts only for anything that leaves my machine.

Three rules you actually use beat thirty you aspired to.

docs.title: Split them once there are more than a dozen
docs.text:
A single file of forty rules gets skimmed. At that point, break them into topic files — one for how you write, one for how projects are organised, one per integration that has a quirk — and have the instruction file point at them. The agent loads the relevant one when the subject comes up.

Keep the genuinely load-bearing ones inline, where they can't be missed:

Sending email: show me the draft. Never send directly.
Meeting logs: newest entry at the top.

A real annotated example

docs.title: What makes a rule hold
docs.text:
This is the part that surprised me, and it runs against instinct.

Shouting makes rules weaker, not stronger. CRITICAL: YOU MUST NEVER reads as emphasis to you and as noise to the model. When everything is critical, nothing is. Strip the ceremony and the real constraints start standing out again.

Say what to do, not only what to avoid. "Write in flowing prose with no headers or bullets" works better than "don't use markdown". When you do have to forbid something, pair the ban with the thing you want instead.

Use action verbs, not adjectives. "Be thorough" is empty. "Compare this against the pre-registration and list every discrepancy" is a rule that can actually be followed — or visibly not followed, which is just as useful.

The full version of this argument

docs.title: Rules are not a safety system
docs.text:
A rule is an instruction the agent will almost always follow. It is not a mechanism that prevents anything.

If the consequence of a rule being missed is real — mail sent, a file overwritten, data leaving your machine — put a permission behind it as well, not just a sentence. The permissions step is what actually stops an action; rules shape behaviour inside whatever permissions allow.

That distinction is the same one the newcomer checklist makes about plan mode: asking for a plan is a request, and the mode is the thing that enforces it.

docs.title: Revisit them when they stop earning their place
docs.text:
Rules accumulate. Some were written for a quirk that has since been fixed, and a rule that no longer applies is just context being burned on every session.

Keeping your setup current

My agent is now ruled.

docs.title: Teaching AI your voice
docs.text:
A draft can be accurate and still sound wrong. It may explain too little, sound too formal for the reader, or bury the decision under polished paragraphs. A useful voice pack captures those choices and, most importantly, helps your AI sound more like you, the human.

Start a voice project. Give it a name and a home in your app, just as you would any other project. It will hold your writing samples and two kinds of guidance: a core voice guide for the habits that stay consistent across your writing, and separate guides for different kinds of writing, such as email and long-form prose. Together, these make up your voice pack.

The starting point is gathering basic evidence so the AI sounds a little bit like you. Over time, it should sound a lot more like you. That comes from correcting it on real work. Build the pack here, then set up the system that learns from your edits.

Ask your AI to help you build it. Open a local Claude Code or Codex session and start with:

Walk me through the voice pack guide at claudeblattman.com. Ask me for the inputs you need first, then help me build it.

Congratulations! You now have an AI converging towards you. Page two shows how to make your corrections useful next time.

docs.title: 1. Start a voice project and point it at your corpus
docs.text:
Create a folder and open it as a project in Claude Code or Codex. If you need the steps, use the project setup in the first-session guide.

The first step is to build a collection of pieces you’ve written and would still stand behind. I refer to this collection as my corpus and name the folder corpus accordingly. Because I do so many different kinds of writing, and they all sound different, I organize my corpus into subcategories of writing. For example:

My voice/
└── corpus/
    ├── emails/
    │   ├── README.md
    │   └── team-update.txt
    ├── proposals/
    │   ├── README.md
    │   └── grant-proposal.docx
    └── op-eds/
        ├── README.md
        └── published-column.pdf

Alternatively, you could leave writing in its existing project folders. Ask the agent to make a corpus-index.md in your voice project that records the file paths and the same audience notes described below. The important thing is that it can find and read the sources.

For emails, ask the agent to start with a random sample of 100 sent messages. Emails are so varied that a handful of favorites may miss much of your writing style. A random sample gives the agent a broader starting point across recipients, purposes, thread lengths, and how much the reader already knows. Look at what it found and add examples of any important kind of email it missed.

Ask the agent to help gather email samples

I had agents take random samples of hundreds of emails. If your agent has an email connection, it can do the gathering for you:

Help me build my email corpus. Ask me what date range to use, then select a random sample of 100 sent messages I wrote, or all available messages if there are fewer. Keep my words separate from quoted replies and signatures, but retain enough thread context to understand the message. Save the samples and source references in my voice project. Tell me which audiences and kinds of email are represented and which seem missing. Flag uncertain authorship and ask me about AI assistance you cannot establish.

If it cannot access your email, give it an export or a set of messages to work from.

I've built my corpus.

docs.title: 2. Explain what each sample was trying to do
docs.text:
