docs.title: A Real CLAUDE.md — Annotated Example
docs.text:
This is a sanitized version of my actual production CLAUDE.md — the file that runs my daily workflow. Personal details (email addresses, phone numbers, specific RA names) have been redacted, but the structure, logic, and scope are real.

Why this matters: The template shows the skeleton. This shows a working system. Study the differences — the template has 20 lines; this has 150+. That gap represents months of iteration.

# [Your Name] - Global Claude Code Instructions

## Who I Am
Professor of [field] at [University].

**Primary work involves:**
- Managing 10-20 active research projects simultaneously
- Writing academic research papers (LaTeX/Overleaf)
- Managing teams of research assistants
- Communicating research to general audiences
- Handling high-volume communications

## Contact & Accounts
- **Primary Gmail**: [your-email]@gmail.com
- **Work email**: [your-email]@university.edu (forwards to Gmail)

## Claude's Role
Act as my top-line **project manager, research manager, and executive
assistant**. Be proactive, organized, and help me stay on top of complex,
distributed workflows.

---

## Current Priorities

1. **Project management**: Create living documents and workflows that track
   everything — status, history, decisions, next steps. A single source
   of truth.
2. **Draft and edit papers**: Help with academic writing and editing.
3. **Meeting integration**: Work with Granola transcripts to maintain
   project records.

---

## Working Style Preferences

- **Minimize permission prompts** — common operations are pre-approved
- **Dictation input** — I use Wispr Flow, so inputs may be conversational
- **Learning mode** — I'm currently learning Claude Code; explain
  capabilities when relevant

### Confirmation Guidelines

**DO ask for confirmation before:**
- Sending emails or external messages
- Writing to Google Docs
- Destructive operations (deleting files, overwriting without backup)

**DO NOT ask for confirmation:**
- After I give clear instructions — just execute them
- After I approve a plan — proceed to implementation
- For routine file operations
- After errors — retry unless the error suggests a fundamental problem

**When in doubt:** Bias toward action.

---

## Technology Stack & File Locations

| System | What's Stored | Access Method |
|--------|--------------|---------------|
| **Dropbox** | Home base. Active projects, papers | Local filesystem |
| **Box** (University) | Sensitive research data, IRB | Box Drive filesystem |
| **GitHub** | Code repositories | `gh` CLI |
| **Overleaf** | Paper drafts, slides (LaTeX) | GitHub CLI + local clones |
| **Google Docs/Sheets** | Collaborative project docs | MCP integration |
| **Gmail** | All email | MCP integration |
| **Calendar** | Mixed Google + iCloud | MCP (Google only) |
| **Granola** | Meeting transcripts | MCP + local exports |

---

## Key Directories
~/Dropbox/Claude/ ├── Settings/ # Global config (synced via symlinks) │ ├── CLAUDE.md # This file │ ├── settings.json # Permissions │ ├── commands/ # Skills/slash commands │ ├── rules/ # Modular guidelines + core voice file │ └── voice/ # Context-specific voice registers (optional) ├── Guidelines_and_preferences/ │ ├── my_prompt_preferences.md │ └── skill-building/ └── Projects/ # Working directories 
---

## Modular Rules

Detailed instructions split into topic files:

| Rule File | Topics Covered |
|-----------|---------------|
| `core-voice.md` | Writing voice invariants — claim-first stance, active voice, AI ban list |
| `email-voice.md` | Email tone, signature blocks, frequent recipients |
| `project-management.md` | Document structure, meeting log conventions |
| `integration-notes.md` | All MCP integrations, workarounds |
| `ra-management.md` | Current RAs, WhatsApp groups |
| `tool-limitations.md` | When to use which AI tool |

**Inline triggers** (critical directives):
- **Sending email**: Use send-email.py — the MCP can only draft
- **Overleaf/LaTeX**: Use `gh` CLI, not MCP
- **Meeting logs**: Meetings go at TOP, reverse chronological order

---

## Communication Style

- Be concise and direct
- Use tables and structured formats for complex information
- Flag uncertainties clearly rather than guessing
- When I dictate conversationally, extract the actionable request

---

docs.title: What to Notice
docs.text:
The Confirmation Guidelines section is the most-iterated part of this file. Getting the balance right — when Claude should act vs. ask — took weeks. Start permissive and tighten.

The Modular Rules pattern keeps this file under 200 lines. Without it, it would be 800+. Each rule file handles a specific domain and only loads when relevant.

The Technology Stack table gives Claude a map of your entire digital life. Without it, Claude guesses where files are and gets it wrong.

The Inline Triggers are the most important lines in the file. They override default behavior for actions where getting it wrong has consequences (sending emails, writing to shared docs).

What's NOT here: Specific project details go in project-level CLAUDE.md files, not this global one. This file describes how you work. Project files describe what you're working on.

docs.title: Start From the Template
docs.text:
This example shows where you can end up after months of iteration. Don't try to build this on day one.

Start with the template — fill in the basics, use Claude Code for a week, then come back here for inspiration on what to add next.

docs.title: Skill Patterns & Conventions
docs.text: Extracted from 20 production skills + best practices from Anthropic's skill-building guide, @rohit4verse's overview, and internal quality rubrics.

docs.title: 1. Policy-First Architecture
docs.text: Every non-trivial skill reads config/policy files before doing anything: - A policies/ directory — VIP lists, skip-inbox rules, calendar IDs - A config/ directory — Label IDs, vendor domains, classification rules - Config is the source of truth; the skill body describes workflow, not data

docs.title: 2. Config/State Separation
docs.text:
• Config files (read-only during execution): Classification rules, label mappings, policy lists
  • State files (read/write): Processing history, deduplication, thrash detection — stored in state/ with schema_version field, pruned >30 days

docs.title: 3. Graceful Degradation
docs.text:
No skill blocks if one source is unavailable. Pattern: 

Collect from Source A → if fails: "Note unavailable, continue"
Collect from Source B → if fails: "Note unavailable, continue"
Report which sources succeeded/failed in metadata

docs.title: 4. Pre-Approved Tools
docs.text: Complex skills declare upfront: "DO NOT use Task agents or ToolSearch. All required tools are pre-approved. Call them directly." This eliminates permission prompts and speeds execution.

docs.title: 5. Phased Execution
docs.text: Most skills follow: Pre-checks → Collect → Process → Report - Numbered steps (Step 0, Step 1, ...) - Clear inputs/outputs per step - Pre-checks verify dependencies exist before main logic

docs.title: 6. Confirmation Gates
docs.text: Three tiers: - Auto-apply (morning-brief triage) — pre-approved policy exception - Batch confirm (todoq, triage-reminders) — show proposed actions, apply in bulk - Per-item confirm (expense-process) — each item needs explicit approval

docs.title: 7. Arguments via Colons
docs.text: Standard override syntax: days:N, since:YYYY-MM-DD, month:MM, list:Name, dryrun

docs.title: 8. Output Conventions
docs.text:
• Section separators: ────────────────────
  • Priority markers: red/yellow/green/blue circles
  • No markdown tables in Google Docs output (bullet/sub-bullet instead)
  • Bold labels for scannability

docs.title: Archetype Mapping
docs.text: How 20 production skills map to the three standard categories from Anthropic's guide:

docs.title: Simple / Lightweight (< 500 words, single-purpose)
docs.text: Skill Category Notes filter-political Triage Single Gmail query + label doc-feedback Triage Collect friction points todo-add Workflow Interactive single-item adder

docs.title: Medium Complexity (500-2000 words, multi-step)
docs.text: Skill Category Notes todo-queue Workflow Gmail search → batch Reminders creation auto-read-stale Workflow Age-based newsletter auto-read todo-review Project Mgmt Consolidated review across 3 lists whatsapp-summary Project Mgmt Date-range WhatsApp digest task-from-email Workflow Email parsing → Reminder with confirmation proposal-write Research Checklist-first proposal drafting, plan-mode-aware, voice pack proposal-revise Research Collaborator handoff pattern, conditional reviewer categorization, voice pack

docs.title: Complex / Stateful (> 2000 words, multi-source, stateful)
docs.text: Skill Category Notes triage-inbox Triage ML-like classification scoring, state tracking morning-brief Project Mgmt 5+ data sources, HTML email output, auto-triage triage-reminders Project Mgmt Heavy state: thrash detection, EW mappings, history setup-project-management Project Mgmt 6-phase discovery-to-implementation project-status-update Project Mgmt Multi-source institutional dashboard expense-process Workflow Stateful, per-item approval, reconciliation weekly-review Project Mgmt Decomposed Feb 15: 1,563-word core + 4 reference files (2,203 words)

docs.title: Performance Logging Convention
docs.text: All skills should log to skill-performance.csv at completion. This makes the CSV a comprehensive usage signal for /skill-inventory and /skill-perf.

docs.title: How to Log
docs.text:
Add as the final step of any skill:

echo "$(date +%Y-%m-%d),SKILL_NAME,TOOL_CALLS,NOTES" >> ~/.claude/logs/skill-performance.csv
  • SKILL_NAME: kebab-case skill name (e.g., morning-brief, todo-add)
  • TOOL_CALLS: approximate count of MCP/tool calls made during execution (use ~N if uncertain)
  • NOTES: brief dash-separated summary (e.g., 7-emails-3-labeled, status-only)

Currently only "High-tier" skills log consistently. Extend this to all skills so /skill-inventory can report actual usage across the full library.

docs.title: Skill Locations
docs.text:
• Standard skills: ~/.claude/commands/
  • Domain-specific skills: Can live in their own directories (e.g., a proposal-resources/skills/ folder) and be symlinked into commands/. Use this pattern for skills that:
  • Share domain-specific reference files (voice packs, templates)
  • May be used by team members independently
  • Belong logically with their domain data, not with general tools

docs.title: What Works Well
docs.text:
• Config externalization — Rules live in policy files, not hardcoded in skills
  • Graceful degradation — MCP failures never block execution
  • Safety gates — Confirmation tiers match risk level
  • Auditability — State files + processing logs provide forensic trail
  • Consistency — All skills follow the same phased execution pattern

docs.title: What Could Improve
docs.text:
1. ~~Heavy skills exceeding recommended 5K words~~ — RESOLVED (Feb 15, 2026) - weekly-review was decomposed into 1,563-word core + 4 reference files (2,203 words total in commands/weekly-review-references/) - No skills currently exceed 5K words (largest: triage-reminders at 3,703 words)

2. ~~No validation or testing checklist~~ — ADDRESSED (Feb 15, 2026) - Added a Quality Checklist (see bottom of this document) covering structure, behavior, integration, and testing phases

3. No decomposition discipline - Some skills bundle distinct responsibilities (e.g., morning-brief does calendar + reminders + email + weather + triage) - A common recommendation: "If a skill does 3+ unrelated things, decompose it" - Counter-argument: Our bundled skills are intentionally orchestrated workflows where the combination is the value. Decomposition would add overhead without benefit for most of these.

4. No failure mode documentation - Skills handle errors gracefully in code but don't document expected failure modes for the user - Opportunity: Add a brief "Known limitations" section to complex skills

5. ~~No version tracking~~ — ADDRESSED (Feb 15, 2026) - All 22 active skills now have *v1.0 — date — description* version lines - Convention: single line after title, overwrite (not append) on each change - See claude-under-the-hood.md Module 5 for rationale

docs.title: Best Practices Adopted
docs.text: From Anthropic's guide, @rohit4verse, and @eyaborai — practices to follow for new skills:

docs.title: Architecture (Why These Conventions Matter)
docs.text:
• Progressive disclosure: Claude pre-loads only skill name + description (~100 tokens each) at startup. The full body loads only when the description matches the user's request. This is why the "description includes WHAT + WHEN" checklist item is critical — it's literally the trigger mechanism.
  • Context degradation: Quality degrades around 45% of the context window. This is why we keep skills under 5K words and use subagents to offload research — preserving main-conversation context for the actual work.
  • Prefix stability (prompt caching): Claude Code's entire harness is built on prefix-matching cache. Skills must preserve a stable prefix: (1) Static content first, dynamic content last. (2) Never add/remove tools mid-session — use subagents instead. (3) Never switch models mid-session — use subagent handoff (e.g., Explore agents use Haiku). (4) Use system-reminder messages for updates instead of changing the system prompt. (5) Treat cache breaks as incidents. (Source: Thariq/Claude Code team, Feb 2026)

docs.title: Planning Phase
docs.text:
1. Start with 2-3 concrete use cases before writing any skill content
  2. Define success criteria — what does "working correctly" look like?
  3. Identify all tools needed — MCP servers, scripts, osascript, file paths
  4. Check for existing skills that overlap — compose rather than duplicate

docs.title: Writing Phase
docs.text:
1. Description field: [What it does] + [When to use it] + [Key capabilities]
  2. Put critical instructions first — Claude may not reach the bottom of long skills
  3. Use explicit language — "ALWAYS", "NEVER", "MUST" for non-negotiable rules
  4. Include examples for ambiguous operations
  5. Reference bundled files rather than inlining large content

docs.title: Testing Phase
docs.text:
1. Test triggering — does it activate on natural phrasing? Does it avoid false positives?
  2. Test graceful degradation — what happens when an MCP is down?
  3. Compare to baseline — is the skill actually better than no skill?

docs.title: Maintenance Phase
docs.text:
1. Review periodically — are the policy files still accurate?
  2. Prune state files — enforce the >30-day cleanup rule
  3. Watch for drift — do MCP tool names still match? Did APIs change?

docs.title: Quality Checklist
docs.text: Use when creating or reviewing skills.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• [ ] name field is kebab-case
  • [ ] description includes WHAT, WHEN, and key capabilities (under 1024 chars)
  • [ ] No XML angle brackets in frontmatter
  • [ ] Skill body under 5,000 words (move extras to references/)
  • [ ] Critical instructions appear in the first 500 words

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• [ ] Reads config/policy files before acting (if applicable)
  • [ ] Handles MCP unavailability gracefully (doesn't block)
  • [ ] User confirmation gates match the risk level of actions
  • [ ] Arguments use colon syntax (days:N, dryrun) where applicable
  • [ ] Includes explicit error handling for known failure modes

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
• [ ] All MCP tools called directly (no unnecessary ToolSearch)
  • [ ] State files have schema_version field (if stateful)
  • [ ] Output format matches destination (no markdown tables in Google Docs)
  • [ ] File paths use consistent conventions (~/.claude/ for skills, project directories for config)

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• [ ] Triggers on 2-3 natural phrasings of the request
  • [ ] Does NOT trigger on unrelated queries
  • [ ] Produces correct output on a representative test case
  • [ ] Degrades gracefully when one data source is unavailable

docs.title: Tool Limitations & When to Use Alternatives
docs.text: Claude should proactively recommend other tools when they would serve the task better. Don't try to do everything -- be honest about limitations.

docs.title: When to Use Claude Code vs Claude.ai (Browser)
docs.text:
Claude Code Claude.ai (browser) Working with local files (Dropbox, repos) Quick questions without file context Need MCP integrations (Gmail, Calendar, Zotero) On mobile or away from terminal Multi-step coding tasks Want interactive Artifacts (diagrams, React previews) Long working sessions on a project Brainstorming without a specific project Need terminal access (git, gh, etc.) Sharing a conversation link with someone

Default to Claude Code when at your computer working. Use Claude.ai for quick lookups, mobile access, or when you want interactive Artifacts.

docs.title: When to Recommend ChatGPT
docs.text:
• Deep Research: Multi-source literature synthesis, comprehensive topic surveys, "find everything about X"
  • Web-heavy tasks: Current events, recent news, fact-checking against live sources
  • Image generation: When I need visuals created
  • Data exploration sandbox: For quick "plot this CSV" or "run a regression" tasks without touching project files

docs.title: When to Recommend Gemini
docs.text:
• Google-native search: When deep Google Search integration matters
  • Very long documents: For documents exceeding 200K tokens
  • Google Workspace-heavy tasks: If MCP is acting up, Gemini's native integration may be smoother
  • Spreadsheet manipulation: For heavy spreadsheet work (formulas, pivots, complex formatting)
  • Video/audio analysis: Gemini can process video and audio files directly; Claude cannot

docs.title: When to Recommend Perplexity
docs.text:
• Citation-heavy research: When I need claims backed by specific sources with links
  • Quick factual lookups: When I need current, sourced answers fast

docs.title: How Claude Should Flag Limitations
docs.text:
When I ask for something where Claude has a known weakness, say so directly. Example:

"I can attempt this web search, but my results will be limited. For comprehensive research on [topic], ChatGPT's Deep Research or Perplexity would give you better coverage. Want me to proceed with what I can access, or would you prefer to take this to another tool?"

Don't apologize excessively -- just flag it once and offer to proceed or hand off.

docs.title: Additional Limitations to Flag
docs.text:
Math and calculations: Don't trust in-line arithmetic in conversational responses. For any calculation that matters (grant budgets, sample sizes, statistics), write and execute Python code, or recommend external verification (Wolfram Alpha, calculator). Flag when providing numerical results that weren't computed programmatically.

Complex PDFs: If PDF extraction looks garbled (tables scrambled, columns merged, OCR errors), flag it immediately and suggest: (1) copy-paste the specific section needed, (2) try a different PDF export, or (3) use Adobe Acrobat's text extraction.

Spreadsheet work: Claude can read Google Sheets via MCP but isn't the right tool for heavy spreadsheet manipulation. For building budgets, complex formulas, pivot tables, or data cleaning in Sheets, recommend staying in Sheets with Gemini assistance.

Video/audio files: Claude cannot process video or audio files directly. For media analysis (summarize this recording, extract key points from this lecture), recommend Gemini. Claude can work with transcripts if provided.

Scheduled/automated tasks: Claude Code runs when invoked -- no cron jobs or background automation. For automation needs (daily email summaries, scheduled reminders), recommend native tools (Google Apps Script, Apple Shortcuts, Zapier) and offer to help set them up.

Real-time collaboration: MCP can read/write Google Docs, but there's no live co-editing mode. For real-time collaborative editing, work in the document and periodically ask Claude to read the current state.

Legal/medical/financial advice: For legal, medical, tax, or financial questions, provide general information but explicitly recommend consulting a professional for anything consequential. Don't present Claude's output as professional advice.

docs.title: What Claude Does Well (Stay Here)
docs.text:
• Research writing and editing
  • Complex reasoning and analysis
  • Document review (via MCP or local files)
  • Code development (Claude Code)
  • Project management with MCP integrations
  • Nuanced feedback on drafts
  • Working with local file system and tools
  • Long-context analysis (up to 200K tokens)
  • Structured problem-solving and planning

docs.title: Get ahead of the curve
docs.text:
If you can't use agents at work, you should absolutely still learn to use them. Pick something from your own life that you already want done. Plan a trip, sort household paperwork, compare an expensive purchase, or finally get a personal website off the ground. The practice should pay for itself in useful work.

You'll learn how to give an agent enough context, let it take a first pass, and work with it to improve the result. If your workplace later permits agents, you'll have experience to draw on. In the meantime, you might get a better vacation out of it.

Use your own device and personal material for these projects. If chatbots are all you're allowed to use at work, there's advice for that below.

docs.title: Pick a project from your own life
docs.text:
Here are a few ideas: plan a vacation, research a purchase, write something in your own voice, keep up with school or club emails, organize your tax paperwork, or prepare for a health or fitness conversation.

Choose one, or use any other personal project you'd like help with. Then work through sections 1 and 2 of the Essentials checklist with that project: start using an AI app on your computer, then try councils and adversarial review.

Ask your AI to walk you through it. You don't need to learn the setup before you have a useful job for it. Start with something as simple as:

I want help with [personal project]. Walk me through the first two sections of the Essentials checklist on claudeblattman.com, using this as my project. Help me get set up, ask what you need to know, and then let's start the work.

The same best practices apply whether the project is personal or professional. Give it a project folder, explain what you want and what matters to you, and use a council for independent approaches to the task. Then add your own judgment and revise. You know your family's preferences, budget, and constraints better than the agent does.

When you're ready to stop, ask it to save the decisions and next steps in the project. If you've installed the starter kit, /done saves a handoff for your next session. That way, you can keep developing the work without explaining everything again.

docs.title: Get more from the chatbots you can use at work
docs.text:
If your workplace allows chatbots but prohibits agents, use the approved chatbot for your work tasks. It can help you draft, edit, understand documents, compare approaches, and examine a plan. Give it material your workplace permits you to use with that tool.

The same conversational approach works here. Explain the job, give it the context, and ask it to help you think through the work:

I need to [task] for [audience]. Here is the relevant background: [context]. Help me think through the approach, ask me the questions that would change your recommendation, and then take a first pass.

Go back and forth as many times as you need. Tell it what's missing, what it misunderstood, and what you'd do differently. You don't have to arrive with a polished prompt.

Make more of your workplace chatbot

Chatbots done right walks through choosing a model, giving it context, improving drafts through conversation, and saving useful preferences. Getting better answers helps turn a rough request into a clear task, with worked examples and a reusable preferences template. Both guides work in an ordinary browser chat.

For recurring work, set up a project with the background and instructions you'll use again. For writing, give it examples of your voice. When a plan deserves another look, try a review in a fresh chat.

If typing gets in your way, try dictating your requests. For a collection of documents, NotebookLM offers another way to work through the sources, where your workplace permits it.

docs.title: Switch to the desktop app
docs.text:
If you're still doing all your AI work in a terminal, switch to the desktop app. For the kind of work on this site, I'd treat it as essential. Being able to see what the agent made, point at what you want changed, and work in the same browser makes a huge difference to the back-and-forth.

Much of this is possible from a terminal too. What I prefer about the desktop apps is having the conversation, the work, and the controls together—and managing several sessions in one working window. It makes it easier to see what's happening, switch between tasks, and give useful feedback.

Once again, ask your AI to walk you through it. Open the app in a project you're already working on and try:

Help me use the desktop app for this project. Show me the work beside our conversation, explain how I can give you feedback on it, and walk me through the features on claudeblattman.com/starter-kit/from-terminal/ that would help with this task.

The rest of this page gives you a few things to try as you work. I prefer Codex's preview and feedback interface right now, but most of these habits work in both Claude and Codex. You don't need to learn every feature before getting started.

docs.title: 1. Manage multiple sessions in one working window
docs.text:
Keep several sessions going in one working window. Have one agent work on your slide deck while another investigates a question and a third revises a document. The sidebar keeps those conversations together: switch to the one that needs your attention, give it feedback, then return to another while it works. For me, this is one of the biggest conveniences of the desktop apps.

Rename your chats so they mean something to you. In Codex, double-click the session title in the left sidebar to rename it. In Claude, open the session and click its title in the title bar. You can also ask the agent to rename the chat. “Funder deck — revise opening” or “August trip — compare options” gives your brain a useful signpost when you return to the list.

Group conversations by project, pin the ones you keep returning to, and use the sorting options to find recent work. Arrange the sidebar around the way you work.

You can run multiple sessions and rename them in a terminal too. What I like here is how easy it is to manage them together in a single window. See Codex projects and chats or Claude's parallel sessions for the controls in your app.

docs.title: 2. Pick up the same session on another device
docs.text:
Being able to pick up the same work from any of my computers is a big advantage. I move between my laptop, my always-on computer at home, and my office desktop. With them connected, I can find and continue my sessions from whichever device I'm using. I don't have to remember which machine I was sitting at when I started.

Both Claude and Codex support this. Once you've enabled remote access and connected the relevant devices, the apps make it easy to find a session, check its progress, and continue the conversation. The work still runs on its host computer, so that machine needs to stay awake and online with the agent running. That's one reason an always-on home computer is useful: I can close my laptop while work continues there.

Help me connect my devices so I can find and continue my sessions from my other computers. Walk me through the setup, explain where the work will run, and tell me which computer needs to stay on.

Claude can also connect terminal sessions through Remote Control. The desktop advantage is having the sessions and their controls together in the app. See Claude's cross-device sessions and Codex's remote connections.

Cloud sessions: keep working when your computer is off

A cloud session runs on the provider's computers, so it can continue working even when your own computers are off. Remote access to your home computer still depends on that computer being on; a cloud session doesn't.

In the desktop app, choose a cloud environment when starting the task, instead of a local project. Ask the agent to help set up the files and tools the task needs there. Cloud sessions don't automatically have access to the folders or signed-in apps on your computer.

Both Claude and Codex can also start cloud tasks from the terminal. The convenience here is choosing where the task runs and checking its progress in the app. See Claude cloud sessions and Codex environments.

docs.title: 3. Open a webpage beside the conversation
docs.text:
If you're discussing a webpage, ask the agent to open it beside the chat. It could be a site you're reading, a dashboard you're building, or a draft you want to revise. Looking at the page while you discuss it makes the conversation much easier.

Open this page beside our conversation so we can look at it together.
Opening pages and local files

Both apps have a built-in browser. Click the link the agent gives you, or ask it to open the page. In Claude, keep local files in a folder connected to the project; a file link outside those folders may not open in the app.

See the Codex browser guide or Claude browser guide for the controls in your app.

docs.title: 4. See the document you're making
docs.text:
Ask to see the work. If the agent has made a slide deck, open the slides. If it has made a document, look at the document. You can give much better feedback when you're looking at the result: “This table is unreadable,” “The opening takes too long,” or “Put the funding request earlier.”

Open the draft so I can review it while we talk. If this app can't preview the file, help me open it in the right application.
What can each app preview?

Codex can preview documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs beside the chat. Claude can open PDFs and HTML in its browser pane and text files in its file pane. The available viewer depends on the file format.

See Codex file previews or Claude file panes.

docs.title: 5. Point at exactly what you want changed
docs.text:
In Codex's browser, select Annotate, click something or draw a rectangle around it, and leave a comment. “Drop this.” “Make this heading smaller.” “These two paragraphs belong together.” Add several comments, then send them back to the agent in one message.

You shouldn't need to learn the vocabulary of web design to say that a box is too big. It's also how we're editing this site. The browser comments guide shows the controls.

In my experience, Claude's feedback tools aren't quite as ubiquitous. You can leave several replies on its messages or a plan, and comment on changed lines in the Git changes view. But I haven't had the same annotation workflow for website or PDF previews. That's a downside for the way I work. I'd bet that gap will narrow as the apps develop.

Claude also has a separate Docs interface with comments; that is different from annotating a webpage or PDF preview.

In either app, give the agent the whole set of comments, let it make a pass, then look again. Go back and forth until you're happy with the result.

docs.title: 6. Keep an eye on the agent’s browser work
docs.text:
Connect Chrome and the agent can work in the browser you already use, including sites where you're signed in. It can read pages, follow links, click buttons, and fill in forms. Think about the university portal you keep putting off, or the five tabs you opened to compare conference venues.

Claude can control Chrome from the terminal too, and you can watch it work there. The desktop advantage is the workspace: keep the conversation and browser in view together, follow what the agent is doing, and give feedback as you go. The built-in browser is particularly convenient for this because the page sits beside the chat.

Start by asking it to help with the connection:

Help me connect Chrome so you can work in my open tabs. Do the setup you can, and walk me through anything I need to do myself.

Once connected, give it an ordinary task: “Compare the venues in these tabs against our dates, budget, and expected attendance. Put the options in a table in this project.”

For work in desktop applications, Codex on a Mac also offers a small picture-in-picture preview during Computer Use, so you can keep an eye on the app it's operating while you work elsewhere. This is a particular Computer Use feature, rather than a preview of every Chrome session; on Windows, Computer Use operates in the foreground. See the Computer Use guide.

How to connect Chrome

In Codex, go to Settings → Computer Use, install the Chrome extension, and use @Chrome in your request. In Claude, connect the Claude in Chrome extension. Use the Chrome profile where you're signed in to the sites you need.

The browser inside the app has its own login session; it doesn't automatically inherit your Chrome tabs. If you want the agent to work in your existing tabs, say so. For forms, tell it whether you want a draft or a submitted form.

See Codex's Chrome setup or Claude's Chrome setup.

docs.title: 7. Review changes in a pane
docs.text:
When the agent revises a text file, ask it to show you what changed. You can inspect changes in a terminal too; the desktop pane puts the added and removed lines beside the conversation and lets you attach feedback to them. This works for a Markdown document as well as an analysis script.

Try: “Show me the changes you made to this draft so I can review them.” Both apps have a changes view: Claude's diff view and Codex's review pane.

docs.title: 8. Manage your automations in one place
docs.text:
When you find yourself asking for the same thing every week, ask the agent to schedule it. Scheduling is possible from a terminal too. What makes the desktop apps useful is having your scheduled tasks and their results together in one place. For example:

Every Friday at 3 p.m., review this project's updates and prepare a brief for Monday: decisions made, open questions, and what needs my attention. Save it in this project folder.

Open the app's Scheduled section to find your automations, adjust their instructions or timing, and inspect previous runs. Open a run's conversation to ask follow-up questions or keep working on its result. Refine the instructions after the first run, just as you would for any other task.

What needs to stay running?

For scheduled work running on your computer, leave the app running and the machine awake and online. A task that needs your local files can't work on them while your laptop is asleep. Ask the agent to explain where your scheduled task runs and how to check its results.

See Codex scheduling or Claude scheduling.

docs.title: 9. Bring several folders into the same project
docs.text:
Your project might have drafts in Dropbox, data in a synced Box folder, and code in a local GitHub checkout. Add those folders to the project so the agent can work across them. The files can stay where they are. Terminal agents can use multiple folders too; the app gives you a convenient place to manage them.

Tell the agent where the material lives and ask it to help connect the folders. For example: “This project uses these three folders: [paths]. Help me make all three available in this session.”

Where to add folders

In Codex, use Edit project → Add folder. In Claude, add folders to the session or its saved environment. See Codex projects or Claude's folder instructions.

docs.title: Other features I've heard about but haven't yet tried
docs.text:
LaTeX editor. Codex has a local LaTeX editor and compiler with a PDF preview beside the conversation. It doesn't replace my Overleaf collaboration setup, but I'm excited to try the editing interface.

Record and replay. Demonstrate a recurring task on your computer and let the AI turn it into a reusable skill—for example, downloading a monthly report or filing an expense. OpenAI calls this Record & Replay, available on Mac. Claude has Record a skill in Cowork on Mac for Pro, Max, and Team users. Both create a skill you can review and refine, rather than simply replaying an identical series of clicks.

docs.title: Your first session
docs.text:
Pick something you actually want to get done. A family trip to plan, or a decision at work where the information is scattered across a dozen files. You’ll learn more by getting an answer that matters to you.

You don’t need to code or use a terminal. You do need to give the agent a runway: point it in the right direction, supply the information it needs, and keep correcting the course. The aim is to get the plane to take off and land.

docs.title: 1. Choose an agent
docs.text:
Start with Claude Code or Codex, OpenAI’s agent. If you already use one, keep it. If you already pay for Claude or ChatGPT, check what your plan includes before buying something else. You can add a second AI later.

The guide to choosing an agent has more detail. For today, the useful decision is which app you’ll open and use.

I’ve chosen an agent.

docs.title: 2. Install the app
docs.text:
Use the official Claude download page or OpenAI desktop guide. Download the version for your computer, install it, and sign in.

In Claude, open the Code tab. In OpenAI’s desktop app, select Codex if the app opens in ChatGPT. You want the part of the app that can work with a folder on your computer.

I’ve installed the app and opened its agent workspace.

docs.title: 3. Set permissions
docs.text:
Permissions control what the agent can read or change and when it asks you first. Claude and Codex offer similar choices, though the names and boundaries differ. Ask:

Help me understand the permissions for this session. What can you read and change, and which actions will ask me first? Walk me through the controls in this app. I want to work in my project folder and keep important decisions with me.
What do the permission modes mean?

Use the permissions control below the message box. Here’s the short version; available options can vary by version and organization.

Claude Code Codex What it means Manual Ask for approval You review permission requests. Claude asks before edits and commands; Codex already allows work inside the project and asks before crossing its access boundary. Accept edits No exact equivalent Claude allows file edits and common file commands, but asks before other commands. Codex’s Ask for approval already permits project edits and commands within its limits. Auto Approve for me Automatic checks handle routine approval decisions. Some actions still need you. In Codex, the project’s access limits stay in place. Bypass permissions Full access Removes major approval or access restrictions. These are broader than automatic review; they are not needed just to reduce routine prompts.

Planning is a separate choice. Claude’s Plan mode explores and proposes an approach without editing your source files. In Codex, ask the agent to show you a read-only setting if you want to prevent edits. Simply asking for a plan in a message does not change permissions.

For more detail, see the Claude permission guide or Codex permission guide.

Anecdotally, I think Auto in Claude or Approve for me in Codex is the right permission setting for most users. For folders and documents I don’t want the agent to have access to, I keep them in the cloud and not locally synced. I also keep them out of the cloud connections I give the agent access to.

I understand the access and approval settings for this session.

docs.title: 4. Pick a project and open its folder
docs.text:
A folder is your project’s home. Always work in a project.

My project folders are relatively coarse. I typically have one for each research project I’m working on, one for AI workflows, and one for family, home, and personal matters. You can nest sub-projects inside those folders. For example, I might keep a Family vacation folder inside Home. When I want to work on the vacation, I point the agent to that subfolder rather than the broader Home folder.

Open the top-level folder for the work you want to do. For a whole research project, that means the folder containing its writing, figures, and other subfolders. For the family vacation, it means the vacation folder. Give the agent the project’s home, rather than opening one file at a time.

You can also organize work into projects in the Claude and Codex apps and give a working session access to multiple folders. For example, one of my research assistants might have a Codex project for a research study that brings together:

  • A Dropbox folder for project management and writing.
  • A local GitHub repository folder for code.
  • A Box folder for data.

Those folders can stay where they are. Add their locally available folders to the same project or session so the agent can work across them.

ClaudeCodex

Start a local Code session and select your project folder below the message box. To add another folder during the session, use + → Add folder. You can also save a multi-folder environment for later sessions. See Claude’s folder controls for details.

Add a local project and attach its folder. Use Edit project → Add folder to attach more folders, and Make primary to choose where new chats start. Start a new chat inside that project. See Projects and chats for the current controls.

I’ve opened my project and attached its working folders.

docs.title: 5. Tell it what you need and let it ask questions
docs.text:
Explain the result you want, the decision you need to make, and your constraints. Point to the relevant files. Then have it grill you about the information it still needs. You can dictate this in whatever order it comes to you.

Not sure what type of task to start with? Here are a few ideas: plan a family vacation, organize your health and fitness, compare options for a household purchase, prepare for a meeting and draft the follow-up, catch up on a research or work project, or review your week and decide what to tackle next.

Here are two examples of how to ask. Use the one closer to your work, or substitute your own task.

A funder presentationA family trip 
I need help building a slide deck for a funder. My initial rough thoughts, figures, and earlier proposals are scattered throughout this folder. My previous correspondence with them is in Gmail. The slide deck should be about 20 slides. Read the relevant material and help me think through what the right structure and flow would be. Is there any other information you need from me, or that we need to gather? Ask me the questions that would change your recommendation. Once you’ve suggested a rough flow, you can take the first pass at building it in PowerPoint.

Help me plan a family trip. Start with the general notes in this folder about my typical budgets and what we like doing. The whole family is coming and we’re thinking about going sometime in August, but our dates are flexible. Before we start searching options, ask what else you need to know about us. Help me compare a few realistic options and decide which trade-offs matter.

For either task, the first exchange helps the agent understand the job. It should come back with questions, an approach, or an initial piece of work you can react to.

For the highest quality work, I use a council of agents to approach the job independently, then synthesize the dominant approaches. You can read more in the council guide, the second step in the starter guide.

I’ve explained a meaningful task and supplied the context it needs.

docs.title: 6. Work back and forth
docs.text:
Some people plan and execute. Other people iterate back and forth. Either way, get used to having the conversation. You supply information, answer questions, read what the agent produces, and give it another direction.

If the proposed flow for the funder deck is unclear, ask:

Walk me through the story you’re proposing for this deck. What should the funder understand by the end, and what are we asking them to support? Use our previous correspondence to explain why you chose this emphasis. What’s missing before you build the slides?

When it produces a draft, tell it what you don’t like and what you do like. Be specific about what needs to change. For the funder deck:

The opening is too abstract. Start with the problem the funder cares about and move the background later. Keep the results figure, but simplify the labels and explain the takeaway in the slide title. Use our latest email exchange to make the funding ask more concrete. Revise the PowerPoint and keep it to about 20 slides.

Open the PowerPoint itself. Look at the flow, figures, and slide layouts. Ask about anything you do not understand, and go back and forth until you have a deck you’re happy with.

I’ve given feedback, inspected the revised work and checked the important claims.

docs.title: 7. Save where you landed
docs.text:
Make the second session easy to start. Before you finish, ask:

Save the work in this project folder and write HANDOFF.md with the current status, decisions, links to the files, unresolved questions and next step. Show me where you saved it.

Open the handoff. Tomorrow, return to the same project and ask the agent to read HANDOFF.md and pick up where we left off. Correct anything that changed since you last worked on it.

The work and a useful handoff are saved in my project.

docs.title: Before you use this on real work
docs.text: Keeping files on your computer does not mean everything happens there. Content the agent reads may be sent to its provider or a connected service to do the work. Use your organization’s approved setup for restricted records. For more detail, read how the data flows.

docs.title: Are you asking multiple subagents to tackle the task?
docs.text:
I use councils and adversarial review as the default for essentially every task and every review. Instead of settling for one AI’s first answer, I want several independent attempts and a synthesis of what they found. One agent may see an approach, another a missing assumption, and another a reason to ask a different question.

The habit is simple: describe the task, let a council work on it, add your judgment, and improve the result. Use /council to develop the work, then /adversarial-review to examine the result, along with your own judgment. Additional review cycles are choices you can add as needed.

Not sure what subagents are?

When you chat with an AI in Claude Code or Codex, that’s your main agent. The separate workers it starts and manages behind the scenes are subagents. Subagents are particularly useful when you want to tackle many things in parallel. A council asks several of them to tackle the same question independently, then brings their findings together. Adversarial review asks fresh workers to examine the result independently and find consequential problems.

A skill is a saved set of instructions for your agent. The /council skill prepares the members’ assignment, coordinates their work, and arranges the synthesis. The slash helps you invoke the skill directly. You can also ask in plain language: “Use the council skill to help me with this task.” The agent can recognize the request, load the installed skill, and spin up the subagents.

A plugin bundles skills and their supporting files so you can install them together, once. There’s more on agents and skills if you want it.

docs.title: The working loop
docs.text:
We’re going to start by assuming you have only one AI subscription, and the council skill in the starter kit works by spinning up subagents with different personas to tackle the task.

Your request goes into /council, which prepares the shared brief, sends it to three independent members, and arranges a synthesis. You ask questions, give your judgment, and have the draft revised. Then /adversarial-review brings in four fresh reviewers. Use their findings to edit again, and save a handoff when you finish.

The simple council loop Your request, council, add judgment and revise, adversarial review, check and revise again if needed, then done. Before starting a new request, read HANDOFF.md. Your request /council Add judgment and revise /adversarial-review Check and revise again if needed /done Read HANDOFF.md, then start a new request See how each skill uses subagents for several independent attempts Council and adversarial review loop Your session invokes council: three separate subagents, Skeptic, Pre-mortem, and Completeness Checker, converge on a separate synthesis subagent. Your judgment and draft revision lead to adversarial-review: four fresh separate subagents, Skeptic, Pre-mortem, Completeness Checker, and Chief of Staff, converge on a fresh synthesis subagent. Your session revises and checks, then invokes done. A return arrow allows another revision cycle. Revise again, if needed /council /adversarial-review Fresh subagents Your request Skeptic Pre-mortem Completeness Checker Synthesis Your judgment Revise draft Skeptic Pre-mortem Completeness Checker Chief of Staff Synthesis Revise & check /done Your sessionSeparate subagent

Next: connect different AI models and change your default council →

docs.title: 1. Install the starter kit
docs.text:
You’ll want a council skill to follow the rest of this workflow. You can ask for a council manually each time, but it’s not practical to keep rebuilding the instructions. A repeatable skill gives the agents a consistent process to follow.

I’m not the only one doing this, and you do not have to use my skills. The advantage of mine is that the workflows and guides on this website refer to them, so the examples should be easier to follow. The tradeoff is upkeep: I get bogged down by other tasks and I might forget to update the skill bundle online. Other authors may maintain theirs more actively. Here’s a list of other council and adversarial review skills others have published.

For installation (and anything else): when in doubt, just ask the AI to do it. That’s a general principle for making the most of AI. The rest of the page is here if you’re interested in what’s happening or want more detail, but ideally, we don’t actually want you to follow all the instructions. We want your AI to follow them.

Open a local Claude Code or Codex session, navigate to the project you want to work in, and ask your agent something as simple as this:

Walk me through the councils page on claudeblattman.com. I want to install the starter kit. Then explain to me what it is.

You don’t have to learn the installation procedure before you start. Ask it to install it and teach you. You may still need to click an install button, approve access, or sign in yourself.

If that didn’t work, install the starter kit manually as a plugin ClaudeCodex
  1. Open the Claude app’s Settings → Plugins. In versions with a Customize section, look for Customize → Plugins instead.
  2. Choose Add → Add Marketplace → Add from a repository. Enter https://github.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman and select Sync.
  3. Find starter-kit, open it, and choose Install.
  4. Start a new Code session in your project folder. Type /kit-hello and select the matching skill from the suggestions. The app fills in the plugin prefix. Send it to check that the plugin responds.
  1. Open Plugins in the app’s sidebar, or Settings → Plugins in versions that put it there.
  2. Search for Starter Kit for Codex, open its details, and choose Install or the + button. If it is not listed, give the agent the GitHub link above so it can check the repository installation route.
  3. Start a new chat in your project folder. Type /kit-hello, select the matching skill, and send it to check the installation.

If the controls in your version look different, use the current Claude installation guide or Codex plugins guide, or ask the agent to walk you through them.

Running into an excessive amount of permission requests?

The quick answer: turn on automatic permissions to reduce routine approval prompts—Auto in Claude Code or Approve for me in Codex, where available. These modes check actions automatically, though some requests may still need your approval. Ask your agent to show you the setting, then read Set permissions in Your first session for more about what it allows and how to choose your settings.

What the starter kit adds

Command What it does /council Develops the work with independent members and synthesizes their findings. /adversarial-review Reviews the draft with a fresh panel and synthesizes its findings. /kit-hello, /kit-setup Checks the installation, introduces the skills, and connects other agents. Usually needed only during setup. /ask-agents Asks another connected agent for an outside opinion. /done Saves a handoff for your next session.

I publish some of my other frequently used skills on GitHub. They do not ship with this starter kit, but you can find them there if and when you want them.

The skills and their supporting files are installed.

docs.title: 2. Meet the council
docs.text:
The starter kit’s council uses three independent subagents of the same AI, with different personas, or assigned perspectives:

Persona Its assignment Skeptic Find important claims that lack support and explain the evidence gap. Pre-mortem Imagine the plan failed. Identify the top three concrete causes and a mitigation for each. Completeness Checker Find gaps against standard practice: people who need to be involved, dependencies, inputs, and success criteria.

These are separate subagents, each considering the whole task through its assigned lens.

My own default uses one Claude agent, one Codex agent, and one Gemini agent. I find the differences between models useful. Part two explains how to connect different agents and change your default. You can start here with the AI you already use.

I understand what the three members will examine.

docs.title: 3. Give the council one real task
docs.text:
Choose something you actually need: a proposal, a decision, a draft, or an approach to a new project. Start a session in your project folder, then type or dictate in ordinary language. For example:

/council Help me develop a two-page proposal for a second pilot. We've already done a first pilot. The information is scattered through this project folder, [other locations, such as Google Docs, email threads, etc.]. I've started discussing changes for this pilot in email with [names here]. Some questions I'm thinking about are, [list them here]. I'm worried about [concerns, constraints here].

Council organizes the dictated request under the hood into a structured PROMPT.md. You do not need to dictate in a particular order or arrive with a polished prompt. What matters is giving it the information that will make the result useful:

  • The result and its audience. What should exist at the end, who will use it, and what decision or job it needs to support.
  • The material and constraints. Where to find the relevant files; the deadline, length, budget, and requirements that must hold.
  • What good looks like. How you will judge the output. “My manager can decide without asking us to reconstruct the staffing plan” is more useful than “make it excellent.”
  • Examples and corrections. Point to a good previous result and say what to borrow. If an earlier attempt missed your intent, explain what was wrong and what should be different this time.

You can leave the method open. If you do not know how to approach the task, ask the council to suggest an approach and come back with the questions that would materially change it. You supply the goal, context, and judgment; you do not have to prescribe every step.

My first prompts in a work session are typically 3 to 4 paragraphs. You shouldn't worry about concision, and in fact the more context and information you can give the council, the better

I’ve asked the council to handle the task. My dictated message includes relevant files, constraints, and desired results.

docs.title: 4. Let the council members work independently
docs.text:
The agent you are talking to sends the shared prompt and relevant files—or access to those files—to three separate subagents. Each gets the same question and evidence, plus any assigned persona. They finish their reports independently, before seeing one another’s answers. Dividing the budget, timetable, and writing among agents can be useful too, but that is a different assignment from getting independent takes on the whole proposal.

When all three reports are back, your main agent brings them together for synthesis. It gives that job to a fresh subagent. The synthesis compares the reasons and evidence, explains the disagreements, and brings forward important findings raised by only one member. It produces one report with the recommended approach, the unresolved questions, and the decisions that need your judgment. Agreement alone does not prove a claim is true.

My three subagents ran and produced a synthesis report for me.

docs.title: 5. Ask questions and give your judgment
docs.text:
Read the synthesis. Ask for elaboration or clarification on consequential or debated points. You can ask the agent to bring forward the relevant evidence and explain why the council members disagree.

Explain the disagreement about staffing. Which assumptions drive it, what evidence supports each view, and what would change the recommendation?

You do not have to accept the recommendations verbatim. Once you have dug into the points you did not understand or agree with, say what you accept, reject, or want changed. For example, if the synthesis has numbered recommendations:

I’ve read points 4, 5, and 6; they sound fine. Reject point 1: I want to test the process with our existing customers before expanding it to new ones. Apply your suggested revision in point 9, shortening the pilot to five weeks so we have a week to deal with delays. Save the current version, then revise the proposal itself using these decisions.

Your priorities and constraints help the agent revise the actual work.

I dug into the important disagreements and have given my direction.

docs.title: 6. Run adversarial review
docs.text:
Once you’ve added your judgment, provided feedback, and pushed back where needed, use /adversarial-review to examine the revised work. It starts a fresh panel to look for consequential problems. The starter kit’s default is four independent subagents of the same AI, followed by a fresh synthesis.

Reviewer What it checks in the draft Skeptic Which important claims lack support? Where is the argument relying on wishful thinking? Pre-mortem What are the top three concrete causes of failure, and what could prevent each? Completeness Checker Who needs to be involved? What dependencies, inputs, or success criteria are missing? Which vague commitments need to be made concrete? Chief of Staff What is the actual decision, what does saying yes cost, and is it reversible? Would a smaller commitment serve you better?

The first three personas overlap with /council, but they now review the draft, using fresh reviewers who did not develop it. The Chief of Staff adds a check on whether the result helps you decide and act.

/adversarial-review Review the revised pilot proposal against my original request and the decisions we made afterward. Distinguish must-fix problems from preferences.

Just like /council, each reviewer receives the full brief and the same version of the work, plus its assigned focus.

I have reviewed the findings of the four-member panel.

docs.title: 7. Apply the changes and check them
docs.text:
Review does not, in and of itself, finish the task. Once /adversarial-review has come back, I edit again using those comments and findings. Tell the agent which findings to act on, ask it to explain any it rejects, and inspect the changed files. Go back and forth with your agent as many times as you need to get a final result you’re satisfied with.

I usually find one Council round and one Adversarial Review round, plus a few back and forth final comments, sufficient. Of course, that’s not a hard rule. A major revision, unresolved disagreement, or new evidence may justify another round. Give that round a specific question to settle.

The useful fixes are applied, and I have checked the result.

docs.title: 8. Save where you landed
docs.text:
Agentic memory is getting better, but for consequential work or long working days, use /done to save a handoff in your project folder. This is particularly helpful if you are planning to pick up work in this project in a new session rather than continuing in this one.

/done asks the agent to record the current status, decisions, unresolved questions, next action, and links to the work and council reports in HANDOFF.md. It gives the next session a route back to the task brief, individual reports, and synthesis saved with the project, so it can inspect how you reached the result.

The work and handoff are saved where I can find them.

docs.title: The master checklist
docs.text:
A suggested route through the site's guides and workflows, from the basics to research, project management and everyday tasks. Tick things off as you go, and skip what you already know or don't need.

The stages build on one another, but there is no timetable. Follow the order when you want a starting point, or go straight to the work you need help with. The times beside the tasks are rough estimates.

Use Essentials for the core habits, Projects and research or Work and everyday life for a task, and Customize your workflow for connections, instructions, skills, and templates. The checklist below brings those guides together. Data analysis, coding rules, and academic expenses are still forthcoming; their linked pages are labeled as placeholders.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Set up, and introduce yourself
docs.text: Decide which agent to use: Picking your agent (2 min) Work through your first session (30 min) Build your CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md file (30 min) Decide whether any research tools are worthwhile to you (5 min) Get comfortable in VS Code, where you can see the files you're working on (15 min) Skim the FAQ so you know what's answered there (5 min)

docs.title: Stage 2 — Learn the loop, and connect your sources
docs.text: Learn the session moves first: start-task, HANDOFF, done (30 min) Run a plan past a council on something that matters (30 min) Read The council workflow for more detail on the loop (30 min) Connect your apps — mail, documents, messages (10 min) Start dictating instead of typing (5 min) Start transcribing your meetings into the project folder (30 min)

docs.title: Stage 3 — Get your files in order
docs.text: Set up or reorganise one live project folder using the AI project folder system (40 min) Find something you said last month with search past sessions (10 min) Consider organizing your cloud storage for better co-working with AI (3 hours)

docs.title: Stage 4 — Set your rules, your voice, and your first skill
docs.text: Set up rules and guidelines that hold in every session (30 min) Turn something you repeat into a skill (30 min) Teach the AI your voice (30 min)

docs.title: Stage 5 — Brief a project, and challenge the work
docs.text: Write a one-page project brief for one live project, and read it before you trust it (30 min) Create council agents with roles suited to your work (20 min) Set up cross-vendor review (35 min)

docs.title: Stage 6 — Research and analysis
docs.text: Connect your agent to a dedicated Deep Research tool (30 min) Research a real project question with Deep Research, check its sources, and give the findings to your council (45 min) Set up your coding rules (30 min) Run the data analysis workflow — the agent writes the code, runs it, and you check what came out (45 min)

docs.title: Stage 7 — Keep several projects moving
docs.text: Catch up on a project that got away from you (30 min) Look at a finished example: project dashboard (10 min) Run one weekly review across everything (15 min) Split a big project up with sub-project routing (20 min) Use the pre- and post-meeting workflow (15 min)

docs.title: Stage 8 — Hand over the rest of it
docs.text:
Read how Chris uses his AI executive assistant (30 min)

Use the skill library to set up one, two, or all of these (~15 min each)

/triage-inbox — sorts the inbox and drafts the easy replies /checkin — the interactive daily session that wraps triage /morning-brief — the same thing passively, as a report you read /schedule-query — answers "when am I free" against your calendar /pre-meeting-brief — who you're meeting, what happened last time /post-meeting — turns notes into actions and follow-up mail /goals-review — keeps the goals.yaml the check-in reads from The to-do loop: /todo-add, /todo-queue, /todo-review

Build a fun life widget — pick one or two and actually finish them (~20 min each)

docs.title: Using Claude Code for Tax Season
docs.text:
Claude Blattman — not quite a CPA.

In a former life — for about six to twelve months during and after college — I was an auditor and then a tax accountant. I was not particularly good at it, and I hated every minute. But I learned enough to be dangerous: enough to do my own taxes, and enough, I think, to teach Claude Code how to take the painful pieces away.

This year I decided to use Claude Code for as much of my tax preparation as I could. I used it to assemble my charitable contributions from a sprawling Google Sheet, compile my itemized deductions from scattered receipts across email and credit card statements, and build a Schedule C for my consulting income. Some of it was still manual. I had to eyeball credit card statements to flag which charges were medical and which were childcare. But Claude Code is surprisingly good at the grunt work: sorting transactions, filtering by category, downloading and parsing CSV exports, and assembling it all into spreadsheets ready for tax software.

It also helped me think through some tax planning decisions — weighing different filing software, running a rough cost-benefit on whether hiring an accountant was worth it given how I value my time. What I did in about three hours, I would have had to pay an accountant $1,000 for.

The case study below uses fictional profiles to walk through the skills I built. AI tools in this space are moving fast — expect updated approaches next year.

This is not tax advice

Everything on these pages is educational content about AI workflow design. All dollar amounts are fictional. All examples use fictional personas. Nothing here constitutes tax, legal, or financial advice. Consult a qualified professional for your specific situation.

Don't want to read all this?

Two shortcuts:

  1. Install /tax-guide (below) and let it ask you 8 questions — it'll tell you exactly which parts apply to your situation.
  2. Point Claude Code at this page. Paste the URL https://claudeblattman.com/tax-workflow/ into a Claude Code session and ask it to walk you through the workflow based on your tax situation. It can read the site, summarize the relevant parts, and help you decide what to do.

docs.title: Is This for You?
docs.text:
This case study is useful if any of these apply:

  • You file your own taxes (or want to understand what your preparer does)
  • You have a complicated return — consulting income, multiple 1099s, itemized deductions, investment accounts
  • You want to learn how to build Claude Code skills for document-heavy workflows
  • You're curious about where AI actually helps with sensitive personal tasks — and where it fails

You do not need to:

  • Use Claude Code for your own taxes (many shouldn't — see When to Get Help)
  • Know anything about tax law
  • Have any prior Claude Code experience (though the Build Your Own section assumes familiarity with skills)
