docs.title: Organizing Your Cloud Storage with Claude Code: A Practical Guide
docs.text: Based on a real multi-day workflow organizing files across Dropbox, Google Drive, Box, and local disk

docs.title: What This Guide Covers
docs.text:
If you're a professional or academic with files scattered across multiple cloud services — Dropbox, Google Drive, Box, iCloud — and your laptop's hard drive is running out of space, this guide walks you through using Claude Code to audit, clean up, and create lasting cross-platform awareness of where everything lives.

Total time investment: ~4-6 hours across several sessions, spread over 1-2 days.

What you'll accomplish: - Free significant disk space (in our case: from 19 GB free to 500+ GB free on a 1 TB drive) - Catalog everything across cloud services into a single inventory file - Clean up junk from Google Drive and other platforms - Create a cross-platform strategy so your AI assistant knows where to find things - Investigate integration options for services without existing API access

docs.title: What You're Doing
docs.text: Before touching cloud services, figure out where space is going on your actual hard drive. Claude Code can scan your filesystem using shell commands — no API setup needed.

docs.title: The Approach
docs.text:
Create a working directory for the project. For example, ~/Documents/cloud-storage-audit/ works well and keeps results easy to find.

Ask Claude Code to scan major directories outside your main cloud sync folder:

Scan my local filesystem to find where my non-Dropbox disk space is going.
Check ~/Library, /Applications, ~/Downloads, hidden directories, and
anything else that looks large. Find the top 50 largest files outside
my Dropbox folder. Present a ranked list of quick wins — things likely
safe to delete with estimated space recoverable.

docs.title: What Claude Code Does
docs.text:
• Runs du -sh on major directories to build a size breakdown
  • Checks macOS-specific space hogs: ~/Library/Caches/, ~/Library/Application Support/, iOS backups, Time Machine snapshots
  • Finds the largest individual files outside your cloud sync folders
  • Audits your Downloads folder for stale files
  • Produces a ranked "quick wins" report with safe-to-delete items

docs.title: What We Found (example)
docs.text: Our audit uncovered a parental monitoring app (Qustodio) silently storing 79 GB of iOS device backups, a 4 GB Chrome machine learning model, and various stale caches. The single biggest discovery — the hidden backup directory — would never have been found through normal browsing.

docs.title: Key Lesson
docs.text: Hidden directories are where the real bloat lives. Apps like backup tools, development environments, and messaging apps store data in dot-prefixed folders (~/.app-name/) that don't show up in Finder. Claude Code's filesystem access finds these instantly.

docs.title: Phase 2: Cloud Storage Inventory via API (~30 min setup + scan time)
What You're Doing
docs.text: If you use Dropbox (or a similar service with API access), you can inventory your entire cloud storage programmatically — even files that aren't synced locally.

docs.title: The Approach
docs.text:
1. Get an API token from your cloud provider's developer console (Dropbox: dropbox.com/developers/apps)
  2. Have Claude Code write and run a Python script that:
  3. Enumerates every file via the API (metadata only, not content)
  4. Captures path, size, and last-modified date

  5. Saves raw results to a JSON file for reuse

  6. Generate summary reports:

  7. Top folders by size — where is the bulk?
  8. Cold storage candidates — big folders untouched for 12+ months
  9. Age distribution — what percentage is actively used vs. archive?
  10. File type breakdown — are you storing massive data files locally that could live elsewhere?

docs.title: What We Found (example)
docs.text: Our Dropbox had 630K files totaling 1,407 GB, but only 150 GB (10.6%) was actively used in the last 12 months. This meant a 2 TB drive was more than sufficient — no need for 4 TB.

docs.title: Key Lesson
docs.text: Most cloud storage is archive. Once you see the active-vs-archive split, selective sync decisions become obvious. You don't need all your published papers, old datasets, or historical camera uploads on your laptop.

docs.title: What You're Doing
docs.text: Using your inventory data, decide what to keep locally vs. cloud-only. Claude Code can't change Dropbox's selective sync settings (that's a desktop app function), but it can tell you exactly which folders to un-sync and how much space each will free.

docs.title: The Approach
docs.text:
Ask Claude Code to analyze the inventory and recommend: 

Based on the Dropbox inventory, which folders should I make cloud-only
to free the most space? Prioritize: published/completed projects,
old datasets, media archives, and anything untouched for 12+ months.
Keep active working files local.

docs.title: What We Accomplished (example)
docs.text:
We un-synced ~533 GB of folders: - Published research paper datasets (250+ GB) - Dead/inactive projects (50 GB) - Large active project data managed by research assistants (231 GB)

Result: laptop went from 19 GB free to 500+ GB free.

docs.title: Practical Notes
docs.text:
• Selective sync takes hours for large folders. Dropbox deletes local copies one file at a time. For 500+ GB, expect 2-6 hours.
  • macOS "purgeable" space is confusing. After un-syncing, Finder may show space as "purgeable" rather than "free" — this is normal APFS behavior. The space is available.
  • There are multiple UI paths. If one method doesn't seem to work (Dropbox has changed its sync UI several times), try right-clicking folders in Finder > Dropbox > Make Online-Only.

docs.title: What You're Doing
docs.text: Google Drive tends to accumulate junk: untitled documents, duplicate translations, old exports, and loose files with no folder structure. Claude Code can inventory and clean this up via MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You need a Google Workspace MCP server configured. The community google_workspace_mcp server gives Claude Code read/write access to Drive, Docs, Sheets, Gmail, and Calendar.

docs.title: The Approach
docs.text:
1. Inventory root-level items — Have Claude list everything at the top level of your Drive. Categorize into: active docs, course materials, proposals, personal files, translations, junk.

  2. Identify junk for deletion — Empty/untitled documents, duplicate files, old exports. Get approval before trashing.

  3. Trash in batches — Claude Code can move items to trash via the Drive API. We trashed ~100 items across several rounds.

  4. Build a master inventory — Save a comprehensive catalog of remaining files to a local markdown file. This becomes your AI's reference for "where is X?"

  5. Create team review spreadsheets (optional) — If you need collaborators to help map files to projects, Claude Code can create Google Sheets with clickable links to each document.

docs.title: What We Found (example)
docs.text: Our Google Drive had ~400 root-level items including: - 60+ duplicate translated documents (same source, different dates) - 8 untitled/empty documents - Multiple PDF versions of the same paper - 15 legacy shortcuts to moved files

docs.title: Key Lesson
docs.text: Google Drive cleanup is more about cataloging than reorganizing. Moving files into folders provides minimal value if you have an AI that can search by content. The high-value action is creating an inventory file that gives Claude Code awareness of what exists and where it maps to your project structure.

docs.title: What You're Doing
docs.text: Audit any remaining cloud services — Box, iCloud, OneDrive — to understand what's there and whether it's duplicated.

docs.title: The Challenge
docs.text: Not all services have API or MCP access from Claude Code. For managed enterprise accounts (like university Box), programmatic access may require IT approval.

docs.title: Approaches by Access Level
docs.text:
Full API access (e.g., Google Drive via MCP): Claude Code can inventory, search, and modify files directly.

Desktop sync app (e.g., Box Drive): If the sync app is installed, Claude Code may be able to read files through the local filesystem at ~/Library/CloudStorage/. However, macOS may block access depending on Full Disk Access permissions. Fix: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access > enable the desktop app (or, if you run it from a terminal, that terminal app).

Web-only (no API, no sync): Take screenshots of the folder structure and have Claude Code read them. Claude is multimodal — it can catalog folders from screenshots and cross-reference with other services.

What We Did (example): - iCloud Drive: Confirmed no user files stored there (app data only). Dropped from scope. - Personal Box: Cataloged via screenshots. Found all content duplicated in university Box. Decision: close the personal account. - University Box: Cataloged ~60 folders via screenshots. Identified stale committee folders, empty folders, and duplicate content. Investigated 5 integration paths (Box Drive filesystem, rclone, Box MCP Server, Box CLI, official Box Remote MCP).

docs.title: Key Lesson
docs.text: Screenshots are a surprisingly effective workaround. When you can't get API access, 4-5 screenshots of a folder listing give Claude Code enough to build a complete catalog and cross-reference against other services.

docs.title: What You're Doing
docs.text: Create persistent files that give Claude Code awareness of your full file landscape across every session.

docs.title: The Deliverables
docs.text:
1. Master inventory file (e.g., file-inventory.md)
  2. Saved locally where Claude Code can read it on demand
  3. Contains: Google Drive catalog, Box catalog, cleanup log, cross-platform notes

  4. NOT loaded into every session's system prompt — too large. Referenced when needed.

  5. Updated system instructions (e.g., CLAUDE.md)

  6. Add a "Technology Stack & File Locations" table listing each service, what's stored, and access method
  7. Add cross-platform strategy: "Dropbox = home base; Google Docs linked via PROJECT_INDEX.md"

  8. Keep it minimal — 5-10 lines, not a full inventory

  9. Project index files (optional, per-project)

  10. For your top 5 active projects, create a PROJECT_INDEX.md in each Dropbox project folder
  11. Links to: Google Docs, Sheets, Box folders, Overleaf repos
  12. Claude Code reads these to know where a project's assets live across platforms

docs.title: Key Lesson
docs.text: Don't over-organize. The inventory file and updated system instructions give Claude Code 90% of the awareness it needs. Only create per-project index files for projects you're actively working on — not for everything.

docs.title: What You're Doing
docs.text: Some disk audit findings require deeper investigation — troubleshooting apps, understanding backup behavior, or making keep/delete decisions.

docs.title: Example: Parental Monitoring App
docs.text: Our disk audit found 79 GB of hidden iOS backups from a parental monitoring app. The subsequent deep dive involved: - Researching what the app actually does and what the backups contain - Determining which features require the desktop app vs. work from mobile alone - Making a keep/delete decision with full information - Troubleshooting the app when it broke after deleting old backups (Electron app crash, GPU rendering issue, admin permissions) - Setting up a cron job to manage unbounded log file growth - Creating Apple Reminders for follow-up tasks

docs.title: Key Lesson
docs.text: Claude Code excels at app troubleshooting. It can read log files, check process status, search for error messages, look up documentation, and suggest fixes in real time. This saved at least an hour of manual googling and trial-and-error.

docs.title: What Worked Well
docs.text:
• Local disk scanning — instant, comprehensive, finds hidden bloat
  • Dropbox API inventory — definitive data on active vs. archive split
  • Google Drive cleanup via MCP — batch operations on hundreds of files
  • Screenshot-based cataloging — practical workaround for services without API access
  • Cross-platform inventory file — persistent AI awareness without over-engineering
  • Email integration — sending team emails about findings directly from the session

docs.title: What Didn't Work / Wasn't Worth It
docs.text:
• Elaborate folder reorganization in Google Drive — cataloging was high-value; moving files into folders was low-value
  • Building team review spreadsheets — for 30 files, an email is faster than a spreadsheet workflow
  • Box Drive filesystem access — macOS sandboxing blocked it; needed Full Disk Access fix
  • Complex MCP/API setup for services with low file counts — if a service has <50 files, screenshots are faster than configuring an integration

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text: Tool What It Did Claude Code filesystem access Local disk scanning, reading reports, editing config files Shell commands (du, df, ps, pkill) Disk usage analysis, process management Dropbox API (via Python SDK) Cloud storage inventory — 630K files enumerated Google Workspace MCP Drive file listing, trash operations, Sheets creation, Gmail osascript Apple Reminders creation, Notes search Web search Researching app behavior, integration options Screenshot reading Cataloging Box folders without API access

docs.title: Reproducible Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Create a working directory for the project
  • [ ] Run local disk audit (no setup needed)
  • [ ] Act on quick wins: delete caches, old downloads, hidden app bloat
  • [ ] Set up cloud API access (Dropbox token, Google MCP, etc.)
  • [ ] Run cloud storage inventory
  • [ ] Optimize selective sync based on active-vs-archive data
  • [ ] Inventory and clean Google Drive (or equivalent)
  • [ ] Catalog remaining cloud services (screenshots if no API)
  • [ ] Cross-reference for duplicates across services
  • [ ] Create master inventory file for AI awareness
  • [ ] Update system instructions with file location map
  • [ ] Create project index files for top active projects
  • [ ] Write cleanup instructions for other machines (if applicable)
  • [ ] Investigate integration options for remaining services

Guide created: February 12, 2026 Based on file management sessions using Claude Code (Opus 4.6)

docs.title: Coding rules
docs.text:
Not written yet

This page is a placeholder. It is linked from stage 6 of the master checklist, which budgets 30 minutes for it. Nothing below is drafted copy.

docs.title: What this page needs to cover
docs.text:
• Where coding rules live, and how they relate to the general rules and guidelines that apply to every session. Decide whether this is its own page or a section of that one.
  • Language and environment: which language, which version, which packages are allowed, and what the agent should do when it wants a new dependency.
  • House style: naming, file layout, comments, where scripts go.
  • What the agent may run, and what only you run. This is the load-bearing one for anyone working with real data.
  • How output gets checked before it's trusted — reproducibility, seeds, a record of what was run against which data.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Overlaps N16 in the backlog, which revamps build-your-own/rules.md. These two should be written together or the boundary will blur.
  • Needs the restricted-data decision that the data analysis workflow also waits on.

docs.title: Are you using 2–4 different AI models?
docs.text:
My default council is more than one AI. I ask different models to work on the same task, rather than assigning different personas to the same AI as on the first page. I find that they make different suggestions from one another.

At the time of writing (October 2026), my top choices are Claude, Codex by OpenAI (ChatGPT), and Antigravity by Google (Gemini). I use all three. Start by getting an inexpensive, lower-tier subscription to a second AI for your high-value tasks. Try it for a month, then decide whether it’s worth purchasing a higher-tier subscription to use for all your tasks, or even subscribing to a third. I also have an inexpensive Grok subscription for specific questions every so often.

docs.title: Why would I spend money on this?
docs.text:
Think about the most important thing you have to do this month. How much would you be willing to pay for it to be done 20% better or 30% faster (or both!)?

The value of an hour of time and the value of a task will be different for everyone, but my suspicion is that it’s likely more than $23. It may well be worth more than $100 or even $200. Now think about all the other important tasks you could use it for over the course of the month.

I tend to think about this in terms of the cost of a research assistant: how much more they can accomplish in a day, or which tasks I can accomplish without their help. You can think about it in terms of your own hourly wage, or even how many coffees you buy in a month.

docs.title: What is each model good at?
docs.text:
For councils, I start by treating Claude, Codex, and Gemini as generalists. I want each to take a fresh look at the whole task. I don’t need to decide in advance that one is the writer and another is the critic. I use Grok for specific outside questions rather than as a regular council member.

To decide which earns a place in your own workflow, try them on work you can judge:

  • Writing and revision: which gives you a draft you can actually use, and responds well to your corrections?
  • Research and checking: which finds useful evidence, supports its claims, and catches something important the others missed?
  • Getting the work done: which can use your files and tools, make the requested changes, and check the result with the least back-and-forth?

You can ask your main AI to arrange the comparison and bring the results together. Read the actual work before deciding which subscription to keep.

Continue with the master checklist →

docs.title: 1. Download the apps
docs.text:
Our general advice is to always ask your AI to do this for you. In this case, your AI might be able to help you download the apps using its in-app browser tools.

That said, this is one part of AI setup that I think may be easier to do manually. Download the second app you want to try, choose the version for your computer, and sign in:

  • Download Claude.
  • Download ChatGPT, which includes Codex.
  • Download Google Antigravity, which I use to work with Gemini.

I’ve installed and signed in to the apps I want to use.

docs.title: 2. Connect another model
docs.text:
Once again, ask your AI to do this for you. Keep working in the app you prefer. Your main agent will call the other agents and bring their answers back into your conversation.

Open a session in the project folder you used on the first page. If you have not installed the starter kit, do that first. Then ask something as simple as:

I want to connect the other AI apps to this app. I think there are instructions on claudeblattman.com. Walk me through it.

Or tell it exactly what you want to connect:

I want to connect [app 2] and [app 3] to [main app you are currently in]. I want you to be able to call agents and subagents from those apps, collect the information, and bring it back to this app.
If you need the steps, connect the agents with /kit-setup ClaudeCodex
  1. Start a Code session in your project folder.
  2. Type /kit-setup, select the matching skill from the suggestions, and send it.
  3. Choose which agents you want to connect when asked. The kit checks which other AI agents are available and walks you through the connections, including any installation or sign-in steps.
  4. Wait for confirmation that the connection works before moving on.
  1. Start a local chat in your project folder.
  2. Type /kit-setup, select the matching skill from the suggestions, and send it.
  3. Choose which agents you want to connect when asked. The kit checks which other AI agents are available and walks you through the connections, including any installation or sign-in steps.
  4. Wait for confirmation that the connection works before moving on.

I am cross-agent connected!

docs.title: 3. Ask a quick question with /ask-agents
docs.text:
I use /ask-agents for a quick, specific request or question: check an assumption, explain a disagreement, or give an outside opinion on one part of a draft. I still use /council to tackle entire tasks.

Try an outside opinion on the pilot proposal from the first page. Ask the other AI you connected. For example, if that is Claude:

/ask-agents Ask Claude to read the second-pilot proposal and the concerns and constraints in my original request. What is the most important question my manager should ask before approving it? Explain why it matters and point to the relevant part of the proposal. Tell me which model answered and whether it could read the proposal itself.

Replace “Claude” with the agent you connected. Use the sample proposal or another document suitable for sending to that service. The starter kit’s outside-agent helpers are not for confidential or sensitive records.

Read the response. Does it reveal a problem you missed? If it does, ask your main agent to investigate and revise the proposal. If you disagree, explain why and ask it to examine the objection. For example:

Check that concern against the staffing notes. If it holds up, revise the proposal and show me what changed. If it does not, explain what the reviewer missed.

If the connection is not working, you can still do this manually: ask your main agent to prepare a self-contained brief, including the file paths for relevant material. Paste the brief into the other app with access to the same project folder, then bring the reply back.

I asked for an outside-agent opinion and received a response back in my main agent app.

docs.title: 4. Choose who takes part
docs.text:
The first page’s council uses three subagents of the same AI. Once you have connected other models, I would start with one fresh agent from each:

  • Two connected AIs: one fresh agent from each. Claude and Codex are one possible pair.
  • Claude, Codex, and Gemini: one fresh agent from each. This is my usual preference.

Once I switch to fresh agents from different AIs, I find the personas and narrow assignments less relevant. A generalist from each app, independently working on the same task, gets pretty good results. Each gets the same brief and relevant material, then a separate fresh synthesis agent brings their findings together.

I've decided who my new council will be.

docs.title: 5. Edit your skills to use your new default council
docs.text:
Tell your main agent which panel you want in both skills. For my usual council:

Edit my /council and /adversarial-review skills to use one fresh Claude agent, one fresh Codex agent, and one fresh Gemini agent as their default panels. The agent should call and retrieve the other two automatically. Give these generalists the same task and relevant material, have them work independently, then use a separate fresh synthesis agent. Keep the existing persona assignments for same-AI panels. Nothing else about either skill should change.

Check that my installed skills and connections support this. Save a lasting personal default that survives plugin updates, show me where it lives and how to undo it, and tell me if a requested model is unavailable rather than silently substituting another.

For a two-model council, name just the two you connected. You can still ask for a different panel on a particular task.

Then open a new session in the same project and ask:

/council Run a small test case by asking each agent what model they are. For this test only, skip the synthesis report and report each agent's response. Also show the model reported by each connection, when available, separately from the agent's own answer.

This checks that the agents respond. Their self-descriptions are not proof of model identity. Use the connection's model information to check that. Ask the main agent to test the saved /adversarial-review panel in the same way.

Once the tests work, use /council to tackle a task and /adversarial-review to examine the draft without spelling out the panel every time. You still supply the goal, files, constraints, and your judgment. After review, apply the useful findings and check the revised work, just as on the first page.

My new council is up and running properly.

docs.title: When a connection stops working
docs.text:
Unfortunately, in my experience, these skills and connections need a little maintenance. AI companies keep changing their apps and models, so a connection will periodically fail. The council skill should tell you when it could not call another agent. When that happens, ask your main AI to use a council of the agents that still work to diagnose and fix it.

Check the login first. Often, you just need to sign in again. Your main AI may not be able to complete the other app’s login for you; it should point you to the app or sign-in window where you can re-verify it.

Usually, you can ask something as simple as:

Use a council to diagnose why my cross-app connections aren’t working and help me fix them. I need you to fix the connection to [other app] so that you can call its agents and retrieve their responses. Use whichever agents are still available. Smoke-test the reconnection by sending a small request and checking that the answer comes back here. Tell me if I need to sign in again myself.

docs.title: The data analysis workflow
docs.text:
Not written yet

This page is a placeholder. It is linked from stage 6 of the master checklist, which budgets 45 minutes for it. Nothing below is drafted copy.

There is currently no data-analysis content anywhere on this site — this page would be the first.

docs.title: What this page needs to cover
docs.text:
Shay's framing: "ask the agent to write the code and do the data analysis from scratch… maybe that includes both writing the code, having the agent run the code, and looking at it." So at minimum:

  1. Writing the code — plan first, as everywhere else on this site. AI-written analysis code is exactly the case that the working loop calls out as worth a council review.
  2. Running it — what the agent runs itself, and what you run.
  3. Looking at what came out — checking results against something you already know, not just reading the code.

Candidate scope, from four distinct jobs with different risk profiles:

What it covers Cleaning and documenting Messy file → documented dataset with a codebook Exploration "What's in this dataset" — what agents are genuinely good at Analysis code review The agent writes it, a council checks it, you verify against a hand calculation Replication Making someone else's code run, or making yours reproducible

docs.title: The blocker
docs.text:
The restricted-data question is unresolved. This audience's data is often human-subjects data, and the site currently handles that with a prohibition — keep it out of the folder. A data-analysis page written for researchers cannot just repeat that. It is the page where the alternative route has to exist: bounded tasks, agent-written scripts you run yourself, mock data with the same structure, local models where policy requires it.

Open since the Aniket critique. Decide this before drafting.

docs.title: Are you taking advantage of deep research?
docs.text:
← Back to the master checklist

I use /deep-research to search for information that will help my council do a better-informed job. It gathers and assesses evidence: what others have tried, what happened, and how well their experience applies to my situation. Those findings become research inputs for /council as it develops a proposal, compares approaches, or recommends what to do.

My research workflow uses the same habit of independent attempts: several agents investigate a shared question, then a fresh synthesis agent brings their findings together. I want an answer I can use, with sources I can inspect and a clear account of what remains uncertain.

You can start with research, or ask for it when a council or review exposes a gap. In the pilot proposal from the first two pages, the question might be whether changing how customer requests are assigned would actually reduce response times without adding staff. Research should help you decide what to try and what to measure.

docs.title: 1. Get the research skill ready
docs.text:
/deep-research is an additional skill. It does not ship with the starter kit. In Claude Code or Codex, open your project folder and ask:

Check whether I have /deep-research installed. If I do, read its instructions and check that its supporting files and connections are available. If I do not, look for a compatible version in https://github.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman and help me install it with its supporting files. Explain any missing dependencies before proceeding.

Tell me which agents can do the research and where the reports will be saved in this project.

Follow the installation and connection steps the agent gives you. If you need to connect Claude, Codex, or Gemini, use /kit-setup as on page two. A working connection is one part of setup. The research skill may also need its own supporting files or tools.

My current workflow includes the synthesis. If the version you installed requires a separate synthesis step, ask the agent to arrange that as part of the run so you receive a combined answer along with the individual reports.

Some apps also have a feature called Deep Research. You can use those reports too. Save the report in your project folder and tell your main agent where to find it. The app’s research feature and the /deep-research skill are separate tools, so ask which one your agent is using.

My research skill is ready, and I know where its reports will go.

docs.title: Investigate something you need to know
2. Give it a question that matters to your work
docs.text:
Tell the agent what you are trying to decide. You can dictate this in ordinary language, just as you would a council request. You do not need a polished research brief before you start.

The useful ingredients are:

  • The decision. What will you do with the answer? In our example, choose what to change during a six-week pilot.
  • Your situation. Point to the proposal, notes, and other relevant files. Explain the constraints, such as no additional staff.
  • The comparison. Say what alternatives you are considering and whose experience would be relevant.
  • The result you need. Ask for a recommendation, the evidence behind it, and the questions you will still need to answer yourself.

For example:

/deep-research Help me decide what to test in a six-week pilot to reduce response times for existing customers without adding staff. Read the proposal and process description in this project folder.

Look for evidence on triage and changes to how requests are assigned in comparable teams. Compare the options, including implementation effort and effects on service quality. Distinguish measured results from vendor claims, and look for evidence against the approaches that initially seem promising.

Recommend what is worth trying in our setting. Link to the sources you inspected, explain where the evidence is weak, and identify what we should measure ourselves. Save the research brief, individual reports, and synthesis in this project folder.

Read the research brief before the agents get far into the work. Correct anything that changes the question you meant to ask. If it is heading toward a general report on customer service, bring it back to the decision: what should this team try, within these constraints?

I have asked a research question that will help me make a decision.

docs.title: 3. Read the answer and follow up
docs.text:
Start with the synthesis. It should give you the strongest findings, important disagreements, and remaining gaps, with links back to the sources and individual reports. You do not need to run another council simply to combine those reports.

I pay particular attention to a recommendation that depends on a setting very different from mine, or to a disagreement that would change what I do next. Ask the agent to explain those points. In the pilot example:

You recommend triage. Show me the strongest evidence for that recommendation and the strongest evidence against it. Did the teams in those studies add staff or change anything else at the same time? Explain what we can reasonably borrow for our pilot and what remains an assumption.

Open the sources behind the claims that drive your decision. Check that they support what the report says. Several reports may repeat the same underlying study, so ask whether an apparent pattern comes from independent evidence or from several accounts of one result.

If a source is inaccessible, ask the agent to say what it could actually inspect. If an important question is still unanswered, give it a focused follow-up. Another broad search is not always the next useful step. You may need a document from your own team or a measurement from the pilot.

I have followed up on the important claims and inspected their sources.

docs.title: 4. Use the findings to improve the work
docs.text:
Bring the answer back to your project. If there is a substantial decision or revision to make, give the research to your council:

/council Use the research synthesis and its cited evidence to revise the pilot proposal. Explain which recommendations change and why. Keep the no-extra-staff constraint. Turn the remaining assumptions into things we can measure during the pilot. Point me to the revised proposal.

Read the proposal, add your judgment, and ask for changes where needed. When it is ready, use /adversarial-review to examine it. Ask the reviewers to check that the recommendations follow from the research and still answer the original request.

For a straightforward finding, you can simply ask your main agent to apply it. Research does not commit you to another full round of council and review. The point is to improve the work you came to do.

Keep the brief, individual reports, and synthesis with that project. When you finish, use /done and ask it to record what the research changed, the questions still open, and the paths to those files. The next session should be able to pick up the work without repeating the search.

I have used the findings, checked the revised work, and saved a handoff.

docs.title: Meeting Workflow End to End
docs.text:
Most of my meetings used to take longer to prepare for and follow up on than to actually run. A 45-minute call meant 15 minutes reviewing the thread, 10 minutes drafting notes during, 15 minutes writing a follow-up, and another 10 minutes filing everything. The actual conversation was the cheapest part.

The workflow below automates the bookend work. I still have the meeting. What I don't do any more is remember what we decided last time, take notes, or draft the thank-you.

Four steps.

docs.title: 1. Before the call: /pre-meeting-brief
docs.text:
Run from the project folder 15–30 minutes before a meeting. The skill pulls context from several sources and writes a one-page brief:

  • Google Calendar — the next upcoming event (or one matching a keyword) and its attendees
  • Gmail — threads with the attendees in the lookback window, with snippets
  • Granola — transcripts from prior meetings on the same project
  • Google Docs — the project's living dashboard and research design docs
  • WhatsApp — any recent discussion with the meeting's participants in group chats
  • Local files — handoffs and notes in the project folder

The brief surfaces three things explicitly: decisions required (what needs to be agreed in this meeting), open loops (commitments from last time that aren't resolved), and preparation needs (things I should have read or done before walking in).

The skill has two depth modes: Light (top-of-file brief for routine check-ins) and Full (deep synthesis across six weeks of history for quarterly reviews or a first meeting with a funder). Auto-detection picks by default; light or full argument overrides.

Optional: it can draft a pre-meeting email to the attendees (/pre-meeting-brief email) with agenda items and prep asks. That stays as a draft in Gmail — I review and send manually.

docs.title: 2. During the call: Granola records
docs.text:
I use Granola for meeting transcription. It runs in the background on the Mac, captures audio from both sides of the call (Zoom, Meet, in-person), and produces a transcript plus AI notes. The key word is transcript — the AI notes are a bonus, but the verbatim transcript is the evidence the next step relies on.

I don't take notes during the meeting. That's the point. I pay attention, and Granola captures the record.

docs.title: 3. After the call: /post-meeting
docs.text:
Within an hour of the meeting ending, I run /post-meeting from the same project folder. The skill:

  1. Finds the most recent Granola document for the project (or accepts a keyword or ID argument)
  2. Checks the transcript is real, not hollow. This is the quality gate added in v1.4 — if Granola captured only AI notes but no verbatim transcript (which happens sometimes when a participant's mic fails or the desktop app crashed mid-call), the skill stops and says so. Drafting a follow-up email off bare AI notes produces confident-sounding summaries of things nobody said.
  3. Extracts structured output: key decisions, action items (with owners where stated), blockers surfaced, next steps.
  4. Drafts a follow-up email to the attendees using the extracted structure.

The email draft lands in Gmail. I review and send manually — this step is deliberately not automated. A sent email is irreversible, and every project has meetings where a specific phrasing would be better coming from me.

/post-meeting save also writes a markdown summary to the project's transcripts/ folder. That's what /weekly-review reads from later.

docs.title: 4. Weekly: /weekly-review closes the loop
docs.text:
This isn't part of the per-meeting workflow, but it's where the meeting records earn their full keep. Every Friday, /weekly-review reads the week's transcripts, combines them with email and WhatsApp, and updates the project's living dashboard. Decisions, action items, and blockers that surfaced in meetings flow into the dashboard automatically.

See Weekly Review: the mechanics for how that piece works.

docs.title: What this replaces, concretely
docs.text:
Before:

  1. Scroll Gmail + Google Docs for 15 minutes before the meeting to remember where we left off.
  2. Switch attention between the conversation and note-taking, losing detail on both.
  3. After the call, try to remember what was decided. Draft a follow-up email. Miss half the action items. Send it 36 hours later when you finally have time.
  4. Nothing written down anywhere project-wide. Next meeting starts the cycle over.

After:

  1. Two minutes skimming the brief. Walk in with everything already in working memory.
  2. Full attention on the conversation. No notes.
  3. Thirty seconds to run /post-meeting, two minutes to review the drafted email, send.
  4. Weekly review pulls it all into the dashboard, where it's retrievable next time.

Total time saved per meeting: roughly 20 minutes. Across 8–12 meetings a week, that's a reclaimed half-day.

docs.title: The quality gates that matter
docs.text:
Three places where this workflow would fail without a deliberate check:

  1. Hollow transcript check (step 3). Granola occasionally captures AI notes without a full transcript. Drafting off AI notes alone produces invented detail. The hard stop is the fix.
  2. Email draft review (steps 1 and 3). Both /pre-meeting-brief and /post-meeting can draft emails. Neither sends automatically. Every email is reviewed in Gmail before it goes.
  3. Project folder scoping (steps 1 and 3). Both skills run from the project folder and read only that project's context. If I ran them from my home directory they'd pull six months of unrelated history from every project at once. Starting in the right folder is the discipline; the skills enforce it by reading $(pwd)/.claude/CLAUDE.md for config.

docs.title: What doesn't automate well
docs.text:
• Sensitive meetings. Grievance conversations, personnel decisions, anything confidential. Granola stays off; I take notes by hand; no /post-meeting.
  • First meetings with a new funder. The AI brief helps me prep, but I read the full thread manually too. The stakes are high and the cost of missing a tone cue is worse than the time saved.
  • Lab meetings with 10+ attendees. Granola works, but the transcript becomes hard for /post-meeting to parse into per-person action items when four people are talking at once. I either run it and hand-edit, or rely on the lead RA's written notes.

The workflow is a default, not a rule. When it fits, it fits cleanly. When it doesn't, don't force it.

docs.title: Organize your work around projects
docs.text:
When you return to a piece of work after a week away, you should be able to find its current material, see what was decided, and pick up the next task. An AI assistant can help if the work has a recognizable home and the important files have distinct jobs.

You can do this for a research project, a committee, a recurring document, or a family plan. Start with one project you will revisit soon. Chris's projects in Codex largely reflect folders he already had in Dropbox. He improved that organization over time; reorganizing an entire drive was not his first task and need not be yours.

This guide maps where those files go and how they connect. If the immediate problem is a chaotic drive, see organizing your cloud storage. If you already have a project and need a meeting briefing, see catch up on a project.

docs.title: See the shape first
docs.text:
Here is a small starting arrangement. The names are suggestions; the jobs of the files matter more. A shared document can serve as the current overview instead of a Markdown file. Keep restricted sources in their approved location and put a pointer in the project index.

<project>/
├── PROJECT_INDEX.md          ← Start here: where the material lives
├── PROJECT_STATUS.md         ← Current goals, decisions, open questions, next action
├── AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md    ← Standing instructions for the assistant, if needed
├── drafts/                   ← Work in progress; label the current version
├── meetings/                 ← Dated notes and transcript pointers
├── references/               ← Sources or links to their original locations
└── work/                     ← Dated outputs and session notes

Chris's established research folders are more elaborate. An October 5 inspection of several paper projects found a project index, handoff, session log, project instructions, human research folders, and a separate area for AI collaboration. Their exact subfolders varied. A simplified view of that observed pattern looks like this:

<research project>/
├── PROJECT_INDEX.md          ← Catalog of people, documents and locations
├── HANDOFF.md                ← Current state for the next session
├── SESSION_LOG.md            ← Dated history
├── AGENTS.md                 ← Codex project instructions, where used
├── .claude/CLAUDE.md         ← Claude Code project instructions, where used
├── paper / literature / data / approvals / field materials ...
└── 10_AI_Collaboration/      ← Working notes, transcripts and AI outputs

The second tree explains Chris's system; it is not a setup requirement. His research folders also have a numbered taxonomy that predates the AI work. You can start with one status document and a few pointers, then add structure when repeated work calls for it.

Project entry point Current status and decisions Sources and transcripts Drafts and outputs Standing instructions The project entry point makes each kind of record findable.

The entry point tells the assistant where to look. The status document tells it what is current. The sources let you check why something was said. The instructions tell it how to work. A past chat can help recover history, but it does not replace those project records.

docs.title: 1. Choose one place to begin
docs.text:
Pick a name you will recognize later and a project entry point you can reopen. It might be a folder on your computer, a shared drive folder, or a project in an AI app. The entry point only needs to tell you where the work is. It does not need to hold copies of every document.

Before moving files, ask your assistant to map what already exists: the current draft, reference documents, meeting notes, relevant messages, and any other places the work lives. Check the map yourself. A collaborator's Google Doc or a document in university Box can stay where it belongs; the project entry point can link to it.

Give the assistant the project name and the starting location each time you open a new chat. Do not assume a chatbot project, a folder on your computer, and a cloud connection all provide the same material or share the same settings. Ask what this assistant can actually read.

docs.title: 2. Give each kind of material a job
docs.text:
Material What to keep Sources Original documents, data, messages and references, with a date or version and a way to find the original. Keep restricted material in its approved location. Drafts and outputs The work in progress and finished artifacts. Mark which version is current and whether it is a draft, reviewed, sent, or approved. Meetings Dated notes or transcripts, with a link to the source. Check the record before treating a suggested action as an assignment. Current state A short overview of the goal, people, decisions, open questions, next actions, and links to the material above. Standing instructions How the assistant should repeatedly work on this project. Keep one-time requests and changing project facts out of these instructions.

Your current overview can be a Markdown file, a shared document, or a first tab in a project hub. Choose one place for the status you want the assistant to read next time. The overview is a signpost: link to the full history instead of copying it all in. Date an output that has no dedicated place yet; give a set of related outputs its own dated folder so its parts stay together.

If you use Claude Code, project instructions may live in a CLAUDE.md file. If you use Codex, they may live in AGENTS.md. An AI app's project instructions are another option. Use the instructions for durable working preferences. A changed deadline belongs with the project's current facts; a request to summarize today's meeting belongs in today's chat. How to write an instruction file covers that distinction in more detail.

docs.title: 3. Begin with the record, then do the work
docs.text:
At the start of a session, point the assistant to the project overview and the sources relevant to today's job. Ask it to flag anything missing, stale, or contradictory before it writes or changes the record. If an old proposal and a later decision disagree, keep their dates and sources visible until you resolve the difference.

You can begin with two or three documents. For a meeting, the prior notes, a recent update, and the current draft may be enough to ask: What has changed? What needs my decision? What is still unknown? Connections to email, calendars, or transcription services can help later, but the first attempt does not require them.

docs.title: 4. Leave a short handoff
docs.text:
When you stop, preserve what the next session needs: what changed, which decisions you approved, what remains open, the next useful action, and a link to the current artifact. Review the assistant's account before it becomes the project's current record, especially any claim about someone else's commitment.

Keep dated notes and transcripts for the history. Keep the current overview short enough to read. A session transcript can recover the reasoning behind an old choice, but put the decision and next step somewhere easier to find. The session management guide explains handoffs in Claude Code and Codex. A handoff file does not automatically update a separate project brief or shared document.

When you correct the assistant, save the correction at the right level. Fix a project fact in the overview. Put a recurring drafting preference in the instructions. Leave a one-off direction in the task. That way, a correction made today can help next time without turning every conversation into a permanent rule.

Read the current record Do today's work Review the result Save decisions and next action Return later Preserve the outcome so the next session can begin from the record.

docs.title: 5. Find the work again
docs.text:
Search by project name, or ask the assistant to locate the entry point, read the current overview, and compare it with the newest dated material. When you need to know why a choice was made, search the older notes or chats. Chris sometimes uses a local recall skill for past sessions; an ordinary file search or a direct request to the assistant can also work.

Treat a retrieved chat or old handoff as history until you compare it with the current project record. If the assistant finds two possible answers, ask for their dates and sources, decide which one governs, and update the overview.

docs.title: 6. Decide what the assistant can reach
docs.text:
Start with the material needed for this project and expand access when it helps. Check local folders and connected cloud accounts separately. Also check which tools can read, send, change, or delete. Written project instructions can guide behavior, but they are not a technical permission boundary.

For Dropbox, Selective Sync, online-only files, and cloud connector access answer different questions. Selective Sync removes selected folders from a computer's local drive. An online-only file can download when opened. A connected app may have its own route to cloud files. Dropbox explains Selective Sync and connected app access.

Consider the rules and expectations that apply to other people's data before giving an assistant access to research records, correspondence, or transcripts. You can ask it to help inventory what it can reach, then verify the result and adjust access where needed. Such an inventory cannot guarantee that every access path has been found.

docs.title: Try it on one project
docs.text:
Use this with a project you expect to revisit. Give the assistant a starting location, then ask:

Find the current materials for this project. Before moving or editing anything,
show me where the drafts, source documents, meeting notes, decisions, and
standing instructions live. Identify anything that appears stale or conflicts
with a newer source. Suggest one clear entry point, and tell me what you cannot
access. Wait for me to check the map before changing the project record.

Once the map is right, make a short current overview and try starting the next session from it. If you can find the work and understand its state without replaying a whole chat, the project has a useful home.

docs.title: Project Management
docs.text: How I went from scattered information across five platforms to living project dashboards that write weekly reviews and draft proposals on demand. Built in four layers over several months — each one building on the last.

docs.title: The Mess
docs.text:
Anyone managing multiple research projects might recognize this.

Emails scattered across Gmail and institutional accounts. Documents in Google Docs, papers in Overleaf, sensitive data in university Box folders, field project files on partner servers, personal files in Dropbox. Zoom meetings rarely transcribed — and when they were, Zoom's transcriptions were terrible. WhatsApp conversations across multiple groups. Overlapping projects with no central memory. No accountability system. No way to prepare for meetings without digging through five platforms. Years of discussions with no institutional record.

I'd walk into a meeting and spend the first ten minutes trying to remember what we decided last time. An RA would ask about a decision from three months ago and I'd have to search through hundreds of emails. Proposals would cite outdated figures because nobody remembered which version was current.

I know some teams use Slack to manage all of this. I tried it and it didn't fit my workflow, so I built the system below.

If your team uses Slack or Teams

Most of this system is communication-tool-agnostic. The folder structure (Layer 1), meeting transcription (Layer 2), and proposal writing (Layer 4) work regardless of how your team communicates. The weekly review (Layer 3) currently pulls from WhatsApp, but it works without it — you still get value from transcripts, email, and documents. Adapting it to pull from Slack channels instead would mean finding a maintained Slack MCP server and modifying the weekly-review skill. That's a real technical project, not a quick config change — but the other three layers work without any modification.

The system didn't solve all of this overnight. Each layer took about three weeks of iteration. None worked perfectly on day one. But each one made the next possible.

docs.title: Layer 0 (Optional): Clean Up Your Digital Life
docs.text:
Before organizing individual projects, you might want to clean house. If you have thousands of unread emails, files scattered across Dropbox, Google Drive, Box, and iCloud, a full hard drive, and calendars split across platforms — a one-time cleanup makes everything that follows easier.

This isn't required. You can skip straight to Layer 1 and organize projects on top of whatever mess currently exists. But if your digital infrastructure is chaotic, spending a day or two with Claude Code to get it under control pays dividends.

What the cleanup covers: inbox triage (getting from thousands of unread to single digits), local disk audit (finding hidden space hogs), cloud storage inventory (cataloging everything across services), and calendar consolidation.

The One-Time Cleanup — what I cleaned, how long it took, and prompts you can use yourself

Cloud Storage Organization Guide — detailed step-by-step walkthrough with scripts and decision frameworks

docs.title: Layer 1: Organize the Project Folder
docs.text:
Skill: /setup-project-management

The foundation. Before Claude Code can help manage a project, it needs a structured place to look.

What this does:

  • Walks through an interactive discovery process for your project
  • Pulls core materials from scattered locations into one project folder
  • Creates a folder structure that Claude Code understands
  • Sets up a Google Doc hub: first tab for the project overview and meeting history, additional tabs for core documents
  • Creates a project-specific .claude/CLAUDE.md with team roster, keywords, and configuration

The key artifact: Research Design and Progress.

This is a living document — part research design, part project history, part pre-analysis plan — kept up to date with realities and plans. Partly AI-created from meeting transcripts and emails, partly human-edited when the AI gets things wrong. This becomes the raw material that everything else draws on.

Before you start

Requires: Claude Code installed and configured. Google Docs MCP recommended for the document hub. Time: 30-60 minutes for initial setup per project.

What this looked like in practice

My first project setup was messy. The skill asked questions I hadn't thought about — who's on the team, what are the keywords that identify relevant emails, where do transcripts live. I had to go find information. But once the folder was structured and the .claude/CLAUDE.md was configured, everything that followed became possible. The discovery process is the investment. The payoff comes in Layers 2-4.

docs.title: Layer 2: Capture Everything
docs.text:
Tool: Granola (meeting transcription) + Claude Code

Once the project folder exists, the next step is to stop losing information. Meetings are where most decisions happen and most context gets lost.

What this does:

  • Granola transcribes all meetings — Zoom, in-person, phone calls
  • Claude Code fetches transcripts and archives them in the project folder
  • Decisions, action items, and context are preserved automatically
  • Meetings stop being ephemeral

The shift: Before transcription, meetings were a black hole. Something would be decided, an action item assigned, and three weeks later nobody could remember the details. Now every meeting is searchable. The weekly review (Layer 3) mines these transcripts automatically.

Before you start

Requires: Granola installed (free tier works). A transcripts folder in your project structure. Time: 5 minutes to set up. Zero ongoing effort — Granola runs automatically.

docs.title: Layer 3: The Weekly Review
docs.text:
Skill: /weekly-review [PM]

This is where the system comes alive. The weekly review pulls from every source and produces two outputs: a high-level dashboard and a detailed weekly log.

What it does:

  • Collects data from meeting transcripts, all project-related emails, and working documents from Google Docs — plus WhatsApp group chats if you have that integration configured
  • Synthesizes everything into a project dashboard (strategic objectives, operational status, team to-dos, critical success factors)
  • Produces a detailed weekly log with thematic analysis across all sources
  • Updates the Google Doc hub directly — no copy-pasting
  • Gracefully degrades if any source is unavailable (WhatsApp down? It skips it and notes the gap)

What the dashboard looks like:

The dashboard prioritizes strategic objectives first, then operational objectives that serve them, then everyone's to-do items and critical success factors. It evolved over time to answer the question: What are the strategic goals? How do this week's tasks serve them? What absolutely must happen?

The real value: Week-to-week accountability. Meeting prep that takes seconds instead of hours. A team that stays focused because the review surfaces what matters. New team members who can read two months of weekly reviews and understand the project's trajectory.

How the Google Doc formatting works

Claude Code formats your Google Doc programmatically via the API — applying heading styles (H1 for major sections, H2 for subsections, H3 for person names and meeting topics), bold for team member names, and italic for metadata. This means the dashboard structure is consistent every time the weekly review runs.

The first time takes some back-and-forth. When you set up a new project's Google Doc, expect a collaborative process: Claude applies the formatting it can, you review the result and flag what needs adjusting, and Claude refines. Some formatting — like adjusting spacing, tweaking font sizes for emphasis, or fixing paragraph breaks where content ran together — is easier to do manually in the Google Doc than to program via the API. This is normal. Think of the first formatting pass as calibration.

After the first time, the structure persists. When /weekly-review overwrites the dashboard each week, it applies the same heading hierarchy and formatting rules. The Google Doc retains its structure across updates. You shouldn't need to reformat manually after the initial setup — though you can always tweak if your preferences change.

What Claude handles vs. what you handle:

Claude (automatic) You (manual, first time only) Heading styles (H1-H3) for all section headers Fine-tuning spacing between sections Bold for team member names throughout Adjusting any paragraph breaks that merged during import Italic for dates and metadata lines Custom colors or highlighting for emphasis Consistent structure across weekly updates Tab creation (Claude can't create tabs via API)

Before you start

Requires: Layer 1 (project folder + config) complete. Google Docs MCP. Gmail MCP. WhatsApp MCP optional. Granola optional. Time: First run takes 30-60 minutes (fetching and processing all sources). Subsequent runs: 10-20 minutes.

How this evolved

The first version was a wall of text. Too much detail, no prioritization. Over three weeks I iterated: What should the dashboard emphasize? What's noise vs. signal? The breakthrough was organizing around strategic priorities rather than chronological events. I also had to tune the email filtering — too broad and you get newsletters mixed in, too narrow and you miss important threads from collaborators. The skill got better every week as I corrected it.

See what this produces — full synthetic example

The example below uses a fictional project ("Kingston Youth Futures" — a youth violence prevention RCT in Jamaica) to show the actual structure and level of detail that /weekly-review generates. The project, team, and data are invented. The format is real.

Tab 1: Project Overview & Meeting Log — the dashboard that opens every meeting:

Tab 2: Research Design & Progress — the living research design that proposals draw from:

Full example — Tab 1 (Project Overview) Full example — Tab 2 (Research Design) View as Google Doc

docs.title: Layer 4: Proposals and Reports on Demand
docs.text:
Skills: /proposal-write and /proposal-revise [PM]

Because the Google Doc hub contains the research design, project history, all prior proposals (successful, unsuccessful, pending), and the weekly review keeps everything current — Claude Code can draft almost anything.

What these do:

  • /proposal-write drafts funding proposals, LOIs, donor summary reports, status updates, and abstracts
  • Takes an input checklist (funder, template, budget, deadline) and auto-gathers context from the project record
  • Looks up donor profiles to tailor framing
  • For resubmissions: categorizes reviewer comments and maps responses to sections
  • /proposal-revise applies feedback from collaborators, reviewers, or self-review
  • Both enforce voice consistency through a configurable voice pack

How it works in practice: A collaborator reads the draft, dictates their feedback in one stream, and Claude extracts the actionable items and applies them. Nobody edits markdown directly. The revision skill tracks changes, backs up the previous version, and reports what moved.

Quality assurance: After drafting or revising, two agent-based reviewers provide independent critique:

  • Writing Reviewer — evaluates clarity, argument structure, and voice consistency
  • Methodology Reviewer — checks causal language, identification strategy, and statistical practice

These run as subprocesses in fresh context, so they catch things the main session misses.

Before you start

Requires: Layers 1-3 working. A voice pack with your writing style (template provided). Prior proposals in the project folder help significantly. Time: First proposal draft: 30-60 minutes (including context gathering). Revisions: 10-20 minutes.

docs.title: The Key Insights
docs.text: Two things matter more than any individual skill:

docs.title: Each layer builds on the previous one
docs.text:
You don't need to build all four at once. Start with organizing your folders. Add transcription when you're ready. The weekly review only works because the folder structure exists. The proposal skills only work because the weekly review keeps everything current.

graph TD
    L0["Layer 0: Digital Cleanup<br/><small>Optional one-time reset</small>"]
    L1["Layer 1: Project Folder<br/><small>Foundation — works alone</small>"]
    L2["Layer 2: Transcription<br/><small>Captures meetings</small>"]
    L3["Layer 3: Weekly Review<br/><small>Synthesizes everything</small>"]
    L4["Layer 4: Proposals & Reports<br/><small>Produces deliverables</small>"]

    L0 -.->|optional| L1
    L1 --> L2
    L1 --> L3
    L2 --> L3
    L1 --> L4
    L2 --> L4
    L3 --> L4

    style L0 stroke-dasharray: 5 5

Start anywhere. Layer 1 works on its own. Each additional layer builds on what came before — but you don't need all four to get value.

docs.title: Every skill took about three weeks of iteration
docs.text: None of these worked perfectly on day one. Each one required back-and-forth with Claude Code — adapting it to specific projects, adjusting what the weekly review emphasized, tuning the proposal voice, figuring out what the team actually needed. The downloadable skills are a starting point, not a finished product. You will customize them to your workflow.

docs.title: Versatility
docs.text: This system was developed primarily for quantitative research projects (randomized trials, survey-based studies), but it adapted to qualitative projects with modest adjustments. The core structure — organized folders, captured meetings, weekly reviews, document generation — works across project types. What you iterate on is the specifics: what the weekly review highlights, what the proposal skills pull from, how the dashboard is structured.

docs.title: Get the Skills
docs.text:
Install the project management skills with these commands. Each works independently — start with /setup-project-management and add the others as you build each layer.

mkdir -p ~/.claude/commands ~/.claude/agents

# Layer 1: Project setup
curl -o ~/.claude/commands/setup-project-management.md \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/main/skills/setup-project-management.md

# Layer 3: Weekly review
curl -o ~/.claude/commands/weekly-review.md \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/main/skills/weekly-review.md

# Layer 4: Proposal writing and revision
curl -o ~/.claude/commands/proposal-write.md \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/main/skills/proposal-write.md
curl -o ~/.claude/commands/proposal-revise.md \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/main/skills/proposal-revise.md

# QA agents (optional — run after drafting)
curl -o ~/.claude/agents/review-writing.md \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/main/agents/review-writing.md
curl -o ~/.claude/agents/review-methodology.md \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisblattman/claudeblattman/main/agents/review-methodology.md

Restart Claude Code after installing. For full customization details, see each skill's entry in the Skill Library.

docs.title: Projects and research
docs.text:
For work that runs for months and that you return to after forgetting where you left it. Start with Catch up on a project.

Workflow What it's for Catch up on a project Re-entering a project cold and finding what's stale or contradictory Save and resume work Leave a clear handoff and pick up where you stopped Find past work Recover decisions and useful material from earlier sessions Weekly review One pass across every project, into a living dashboard Sub-project routing Keeping handoffs in the right folder when one project has many strands Deep research A bounded question, real sources, and checked citations The data analysis workflow The agent writes the code, runs it, and you check what came out — not written yet Example: project dashboard What the weekly review produces after a few months of running it

These are stages 6 and 7 of the master checklist.

docs.title: /recall — Search Every Past Session
docs.text:
I kept solving the same problem twice. First because I'd forgotten I'd solved it, second because I couldn't find the session where I did. /recall fixed that.

/recall is a skill that indexes every past Claude Code and Codex transcript on your machine and lets you search them with full-text queries. The skill is by arjunkmrm and is MIT-licensed — I didn't build it. I installed it and use it every few days.

Privacy first

Your session transcripts contain the full content of past tool outputs — anything you pasted into Claude Code, any file it read, any environment value it echoed. Treat the /recall index as sensitive data. Don't share ~/.claude/projects/ or its search index with anyone you wouldn't share the underlying files with.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
/recall uses SQLite FTS5 full-text search with BM25 ranking over the JSONL transcript files Claude Code and Codex write as they run. It supports keyword search, exact-phrase queries, boolean operators, and prefix matching.

It's same-machine only. Sessions from another Mac aren't visible unless you explicitly sync the transcript directories.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The skill ships as a folder that drops into ~/.claude/skills/. Find the source at arjunkmrm's GitHub (the repo name has shifted once; check the pinned skills list there). Once installed:

# First search builds the index (may take a minute for a large transcript history)
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "hello"

After install, /recall is available as a slash command in Claude Code. The skill directory can live anywhere Claude Code looks for skills — ~/.claude/skills/recall is the path I use.

docs.title: Query syntax
docs.text:
FTS5 supports four kinds of query:

# Keyword — matches stemmed variants ("discussing" matches "discuss")
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "buffer"

# Exact phrase
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py '"ACP protocol"'

# Boolean
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "rust AND async"
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "tauri OR electron"
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "auth NOT deprecated"

# Prefix
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "buffer*"

You can combine them: "state machine" AND test matches sessions where both appear.

docs.title: Common filters
docs.text:
# Only sessions from a specific project
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "regression" --project ~/Dropbox/research/paper-X

# Only recent sessions
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "compaction" --days 14

# Only Claude Code (not Codex)
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "hook" --source claude

# Only Codex
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py "hook" --source codex

# Force reindex after you've moved transcripts around
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/recall.py --reindex "anything"

docs.title: Reading a match
docs.text:
Each result returns a File: path to the raw JSONL transcript. Two ways to use it:

# Read the session
python3 ~/.claude/skills/recall/scripts/read_session.py <File-path-from-result>

# Resume the session in Claude Code
cd /path/to/project
claude --resume SESSION_ID

The SESSION_ID is in the match output; copy and paste.

docs.title: /recall vs /conversation-search
docs.text:
Both skills search local JSONL transcripts. Both are same-machine only. The differences are worth knowing:

Feature /recall /conversation-search Indexes Claude Code + Codex Claude Code only Query engine SQLite FTS5, BM25 ranking Keyword + date filter Advanced queries Phrase, boolean, prefix Keyword only Daily digest — Yes (--digest today) Install External skill (MIT) Personal

The quick rule: use /conversation-search for "what did we do last week" style questions that want a summary. Use /recall for "find the session where we talked about X" style questions that want a specific match.

/conversation-search not yet published

/conversation-search is a thin Claude Code wrapper over the local JSONL transcript files — sanitization pending. /recall (the third-party tool above) ships today; the conversation-search side of the comparison is what I run locally and isn't yet in the Skill Library.

docs.title: When it earns its keep
docs.text:
Three patterns where I reach for it:

  1. "I've solved this before." A weird dependency issue, a regex that took me an hour to get right, a shell incantation I can't remember. /recall "specific error text" usually finds the fix.
  2. Cross-project learning. When I've figured out a pattern in one project and want to apply it elsewhere, I search the pattern across all projects with no --project filter.
  3. Recovering from a bad compaction. When /compact summarized away something I needed, the original detail is still in the transcript. /recall finds it; I paste it back into the current session.

docs.title: Limitations, stated honestly
docs.text:
• Same-machine only. If you work across a laptop and a desktop, sessions from one aren't visible from the other unless you sync ~/.claude/projects/ explicitly. For cross-machine continuity I use /done + HANDOFF.md via Dropbox — different pattern, covered elsewhere.
  • Index staleness. If you've moved transcripts or deleted old ones, use --reindex to refresh. The skill is good about this but not perfect.
  • Not a replacement for memory. The index holds session content; it doesn't remember semantic context. For persistent context across conversations, use Claude Code's memory tool or a MEMORY.md file — /recall is for retrieval, not memory.

  • Claude's memory tool — persistent context across conversations. Complement, not substitute.
